That the parsonage .Or the manse is the nursery Of • our cleverest girls is the subject oi an interesting ar:iele by G. A. Wade in the Girl's Realm. Mr. Wade says: "It ,is from ,the rectory, the parsonage, and the manse That th majority, of clever girls do come, if past and present. experience, and special in- vestigations ma.de by me for this .article, count for anything. I have lately been spending much tune in going into the life-stories of most of the women arid girls who have made their mark in our country during the past century, and I think there can be no doubt that, though the homes of doctors and naval officers have shone in giving birth, to girls who have turned out cleverer than most of their rivals, it is .ta' the parsonage, to the manse, to the rectory, to the vicarage; that we must award the palm for standing pre-eminent in this respect." •

They knew that their friend Mr. Matthews was going to fill a larger and more important sphere and they desired rather to congratulate him than to make his heart heavy. At the same time they could not help feeling a great deal of regrets that they were going to lose Mr. Matthews from Warrington. For eleven and a half years he had occupied the position of a minister in a very important church in the town and the fact that he left thee church in a condition of health and prosperity and that he carried with him the affec- tion fine esteem of the whole congregation spoke well for him. But many of those present esteemed Mr. Matthews in a broader sense, in the associations that he had had with other Free Churches, the Established Church, and 'especially in connection with the moral questions which had come up in the town, in which he had been such a power and force. THE WEIGHT OF THE EARTH.

The meteors which fall upon the earth in vast numbers every year add their weight to the earth„ Thus the earth is increasing a minute quantity in weight each year, but not enough to be perceptible in thousands of years.- Except for the escape of light gases from the 'atmosphere there is no known way in which the earth can lose weight.

In San Francisco it was found that houses built On steel frames stool, though the bricks peeled off the fronts. In Japan the question of earthquake-proof buildings has been studied scientifically. It has been found that if the walls of a building rise from a depth of some aft. instead of from the surface they resist the shock much better. Some of the buildings of the Im- prial University, 'Tokio, have been built on this plan, and they have resisted shocks v.-hich have partially destroyed others equally strong as far as masonry is concerned. When residing in Japan Professor Milne had a special earthquake bedroom attached to his house. This building rested at each of its oillar-like foundations unon a laver of a '.ittarter ,or an inch or east iron snot between two flat iron-plates. By this means the build- ing remaned at rest while the ground beneath it moved rapidly to and fro.

div.head: EXTENT OF THE SOLAR SYSTEM.
div.p: EXTENT OF THE SOLAR SYSTEM.

The presumed existence of a new planet outside the orbit of Neptune suggests the furthe4 question of others still more remote. As the peculiarities of Neptune's . orbit sug- gested the existence of a new planet, so the latter when - found may suggest another still more remote. The solar system may thus ex- tend indefinitely outwards to vest and un- known distances. ,The possibility, however, of proving the existence of such remote -bodies with present appliances seems small; remarks the Globe, since even the new planet is only expected to reveal itself as a mintite point of light on a photographic plate.

PLANET WITHIN MERCURY'S ORBIT? Astronomers have also looked for new planets within the orbit of Meroury. When sunspots . were first scientifically o‘cservcd they were, thought to be small planets revolving close to the sun. Under this -impression French astronomers called them Bourbonian 43tars, and, in 1845, Le Verrier, discoverer along , with Adams of Neptune, found a peculiar motion in the perihelion of Mer- curio orbit. He explained this as due to the uttraction of a planet cr planets moving round the sun within the orbit of Mercury. And in 1859 it was announced that such a planet had been discovered by a Dr. Lescar- bault,l physician and amateur astronomer. It wee named "Vulcan," and according to Le Terrier's calculations it was about 13,000,000 ines from the sun, and revolved round it in nineteen or twenty days.

div.head: TIIE PLANET VULCAN.
div.p: TIIE PLANET VULCAN.

No one else seems to have seen Vulcan, and Tet it wes officially recognised-as a permanent 331 ember of the solar system for IR number of years. Astronomers, however, are now prac- tioally certain that Vulcan does not, and Bever did, exist. i Yet. the peculiarity in Mer- cury's orbit which t would explain remains unacc owl ted for !

div.head: FATAL ILLNESSES OF METALS.
div.p: FATAL ILLNESSES OF METALS.

There are abundant chemical phenomena indicating that stability can only be a rela- tiv,3 term, and the truth is probably that no element is absolutely stable. Tin crumbles to a grey powder if exposed for a long time to the cold. The change is known as "tin plague"; the smooth surface of the metal after an exposure to 16. deg. to 45d42g. C. far two years becomes brittle and crystalline. "Tin plague" is even "infectious," for on inoculating other masses of smooth polished tin with small portions of the crystalline raetal the "disease" .spreads, the area affected increasing in diameter from three to five millimeters daily. Tinfoil succumbs to the infection in the same way and becomes -crystalline and brittle right through.

div.head: EATING STONES.
div.p: EATING STONES.

Sir James Ross, in the course of his travels, noted a curious fact with regard to the pen- guin, namely, its habit of swallowing stones. In one specimen he found ten pounds' weight of quartz, . granite, and trap. Other animals, reptiles, fishes,- and mammals exhibit the same strange fancy. In a paper contributed to the proceedings of the Bristol Naturalists' Society, Mr. W. 11. Wicks has .collected a number of facts connected with such stomach stones. The fact noted by Mr. Wicks that the pebbles are usually white quartz is in- teresting, but does not appear to throw any light on the strange habit. Geologists not in- frequently find nests of pebbles in deposits of fine sediment formed in deep' water. To ac- count for these floating tree roots and ice have been suggested as ,agents. Perhaps in many cases the decay of the body of a stone- eating animal might be the real explanation.

div.head: PULSE-COUNTING WATCH
div.p: A PULSE-COUNTING WATCH

A watch invented for the use of physicians and nurses in counting ,the pulse indicates, without mental calculation, the number of beats of the pulse in a minute. It operates on the principle of a stop-watch. By pressing' the push-button a large second-hand is set in motion, and the counting of the puleatione be- gins. At the twentieth pulsation the -motion of the hand is stopped by another pressure of the push-button. The dial accurately indi- cates the exact number of pulsations per minute. A third pressure on the push-button brings the hand back to the starting point. The use of this instrument does away with the necessity of observing the progress of the watch while taking the pulse, and in addition insures an absolutely -correct record. The in- strument is also a chronographic counter, facilitating the making of _ observations, which are automatically recorded in. minutes, seconds, and fifths of a second. A small dial placed below the 12 records minutes from 0 to 30. The large hand records seconds and fifths of a second.

div.head: EOLITHIC IMPLEMENTS.
div.p: EOLITHIC IMPLEMENTS.

After years of heated discussion on the great Eolithic quemtion there eems to be, little doubt, says Knowledge, that, in spite of a few who are still unconverted, eolithic im- plements have taken their place permanently in the archreologists' repertory. Benjamin Harrison has lived to eee his. work appre- ciated, and an army of &Voted adherents willing to fight his battles for all time. Eolithic is a stage rather than a time. Eoliths are sometimes found with paheoliths, for even amongst palmolithic men there were eolithic children; but where, as in Prestwich' Southern Drift, there are soliths and eoliths only, then humanity , was, in three places where the Southern Drift is found, in the childlike eolithic staze, although pcs3ibly elsewhere the -race has reached the palmo- Ethic stage. Mr. N. F..Robarts, calling atten- tion to the native Tasmanian race which died out about sixty years ago, says that this tack- ward race, apparently the most backward race in the world, was actually making eoli- thic instruments before they disappeared.

div.head: WORKIMMEN'S MISSION, BANK QUAY.
div.p: WORKIMMEN'S MISSION, BANK QUAY.
The Unemployment Question.

The annual congregational tea and concert in con- nection with this flourishing mission was held in the schoolroom last week and proved a great success. About 180 sat down to tea. At the subsequent entertainment Mr. James Dodds presided. During an interval the secretary (Mr. A. Tilling) presented the annual report upon the work in conection with the chapel. He said the year has been one of steady consistent effort, and they thanked God for the measure of success which had attended the work. The chapel was very well attended every Sunday evening,as a rule almost every seat being cccupied,and the homely . brotherly spirit existent made the services a real help ; and stimulous. During the year they introduced the ; new hymn book (Garret Horder's "Worship Song ") an undenominational book, and they felt very well satis- fied with it. It has been decided, by the church mem- bers meeting, to make additions to the organ, to pro- vide a greater variety of stops, at a cost of about £64. ; They already had in hand towards the organ extension ; fund £8 I Ss. lid „and the proceeds of this tea and concert ; I would go towards the fund. Trays to the value of i ; £lO have been collected by Mr. T. Dale and Mr. Hough. I ; While they had cause for thankfulness at the large con- I ;I gregations a hich assembled at the Sunday evening ! services, the same could not le said as regards the ' morning attendance, so far. as the adults were con- cerned. They believed that in almost all places of ; worship in the district there was a similar slackness.• I There was no legitimate reason why this should he so, 1 and they earnestly appeal to the church members and ' frietds (especially the man, -aho were tot tied with household duties, as the women were) to aasemble lin God's House on the Sabbath morning. The church membership at the present time ' stood at 77, an increase of 17 on last year. In laddition to the Poor Fund, which had been in exist- ence many years, and was well administered under the I direction of Mr. Thomas Dale, to help deserving cases in the district, whether connected with that or any I other place of worship, it was in November last decided to commence a wider and larger fund, to meet the distress which was apparent especially at this period of the year, owing to unemployment. A movement called 1 the Workingmen's Mission League of Help was com- menced on the Ist December. The district immediately 1 surrounding the Mission had been mapped out, any ' workers appointed to so many houses in each street, 1 any cares. of distress being at once reported to the ' League of Help Executive Committee. As far as possible the workers were appointed to tha streets in which they lived or with which they were best acquainted so that they thus had a good ci pc rtunity of judging as to whether a case was really deserving or not. The fund was opened on the Ist December, and at the present time there were 16 families on the books. Up-to-date the income- had been £l2 12s. 6d., and the expenditure £ll. Cards of membership were being issued to any friend of the mission who were desirous of becoming members of the League, subscriptions of ld.per month and upwards being accepted. The fund was being dealt out on tho broad lines of Christian charity, and 110 matter whether the case reported was associated with any place of worship or not, if it was found to be deserving, it was immediately dealt with. The method or which the League was working would make it an easy matter to attach itself to the Civic League of Help which it was proposed to commence in the town and district. They I sincerely hoped that the efforts of those who were working for the introduction of the Civic League of Help into Warrington might be speedily successful. The need for a thoroughly organized system of relief was never more felt than it ; is to-day. As a church they were of the opinion that the question of unemployment in the town might be taken up vigorously by the town authorities. There were surely plenty of directions in which men who were anxiously looking for work day by day might be given something to do to tide them over the winter and depressed periods of tiade. They did not, of course, wish to unkindly criticise the work of those who give their time and energy to the government of the town, and the probability was that those who N-ere in the background did not fully realise the difficulties that were to be overcome in the setting of the unemployed to work, hut they took this opportunity of assuring those in authority that they would receive the unanimous and hearty support of the chrlstian workers 1 of that Mission, if they devised some means of setting to work, with AS little delay as passible, those men who were desirous of working, and whose families were at 1 the present time lacking the very necessaries ef life. At the close of the year the chapel accounts showed a balance in band of £8 Cs. 80. , The officers ter the present year are as follows :-- ' President, Mr. N. Hough ; vice-president, Mr. George Dale ; treasurer, Mr. 'l'. Taylor ; secretary, Mr. A. Tilling ; organist and ,choirmaster, Mr. F. Atkinson ; communion secretary, Mr. R. Jones ; poor fund secre- tary, Mr. T. Dale ; poor fund treasurer, Mr. G, Dale ; committee, Messrs. D. Hill, W. Worrall, R. Tanner, T. Edmunds and A. Gleave, along with the officials. In conclusion they desired to express their thanks to all who had lelped forward the Nvork of the cl u-ch (especially to Mrs. Crcsfleld, who had, as heretofore, raid the cost of electric Hat and fuel mei in the chapel, S;c., amounting to £2O IBs. lid., and tl ey confi- dently appealed for a continuance of support, believing that their neighbeurhood was tieing continually and permanently influenced for good by the work that was carried on there in the name of Christ.

div.head: SMART SATIN SHIRT.
div.p: A SMART SATIN SHIRT.

The subject of the sketch below is a particularly :smart afternoon shirt of new shape and most attractive style. The original *of this shirt was carried out in soft woollen-backed satin of a pretty ivory tone. This satin, by the way, as I uare- say the majority of my readers know, washes and wears adinirably, and is really a splendid investment if a god quality be bought, for it will outwear three or four taffetas shirts Lad

looks nice to the very end. But to return to our special model. This shirt has a broad box-pleat down the middle of the front, which is ,machincd down either edge, and is adorned with four large, satin-Covered buttons. On either side of this centre pleat, and about midway between it and the sleeve, comes a stitched strap, which is met by a similar strap coming from the shoulder, which buttons on to it about on a, level with the armhole. The sleeves are of the simplest bishop-shape, and are taken into neat little cuffs at the wrist.

div.head: WOMEN \Vim STEAL.
div.p: WOMEN \Vim STEAL.

It is rather disquieting, remarks a writer in Woman's Life,. to realise that many women, and men too, are only kept honest by their environment. Criminologists have expressed the view that female criminals are usually dark; fair women are, as a rule, honest. A woman with black hair, leading a life of crime, grows grey early, but seldom becomes bald.

div.head: KNICK-KNACI:S IN DRESS.
div.p: KNICK-KNACI:S IN DRESS.

Sashes are the mode; the fashionable kinds are made up and worn round the hips. Some cross over the shoulders like a fichu, and are tied 'in long loops and ends at the back. Some surround the waist, and are brought to each shoulder blade. Flat rosettes and tassels—some start on folds beneath the armholes and so arranged round the waist, some falling in one end below the shoulder blade, to the hem of the dress. There •is a new girdle with ribbon threaded through but- tonholes. Many gowns are laced in front with satin ribbon, which has an excellent effect. Huge ruffs are likely, the Queen says, to be worn in the near future with soft mara- bout and ostrich feather tips. A NEW PETTICOAT. .

At the present moment the accordion- pleated petticoat is quite the most correct thing in the fashionable world. These pleated petticoats vary very greatly in shape, some having deep frills which come from a short hip-yoke, and Others frills that set on about the level of the knees. The skirt pic- tured in ozir sketch is of the latter type, and

is of a particularly useful shape for regular wear. It might be successfully realised in satin, moirette, taffetas, or •alpaca. This skirt fastens at the side in the usual way, and is quite plain in the back. The frill is wider at the back than at the front, and the bottom of the skirt is shared in a somewhat uncom- mon and particularly pretty way.

THE REV. J. F. NIATTHEWS.
FAREWELL SERMONS AT WARRINGTON. Presentation at the Parr Hall.

all the things on which Christians agreed were greater then those on which they eifferoci. They could all claim to be members of the true Catholic Church which was involved in the phrase "The union of all who love in the service of all who suffer." (Applause.) He, personally regarded Mr. Matthews as one of the intellectual, moral and spiritual assets of the tomn, , They were all proud of him and glad to feel that he. I had lived among them so long and done such good • work. While they were sorry to lose him they were. glad to feel he was going to a larger sphere of labour where his great qualities of mind and heart wo ald have. fuller opportunities of being used to the best advantage One fact which had endeared Mr. Matthews to aim was, . that he was so intimately fond of English literature. He was acquainted with all the best works of our own authors but his knowledge of literature was not confined to this country, because he was in touch with the intellectual fountains of the civilized _world, from which he, derived a great deal of the charm which had distinguished his ministry. This was an age of dis- belief and unrest, and people were wondering what they believed or whether they believed anything at all. Mr. Matthews had not hound himself rigidly to the old dogmas and refused to listen to the needs of his own time. He had courageously grappled with all the per- plexities of modern belief and unbelief, and had fought , his way through them all. He had a strong hold on ' central truths, and had helped many people in this town ito a similar foothold. Moreover, he was not content to preach the spiritual gospel which would fit people for the Kingdom of Heaven which was to come later on, hilt he had preached a gospel which I was applicable here and now. The foundation of , all soci at reform was to begin with the individual. hut Mr. Matthews' teaching did not end with that 113 wished to give to the people of this country opportunities for that development, to put the human soul in a suitable environment and to remedy the injustices and wrongs which were a scandal and a disgrace to our Curistian civilization. He (Alderman Bannett) WAS not prepared to folio* Mr. Matthews all the way in one particular step he had taken but he could into tell them hew much he admired the courage which 'an ma-le him stand side by side with the Labour party hadjwhat he considered to be justice to the poor. ; (Applause.) Increasingly 00 people of this country were beginning to recognise that that unless Christianity realized that its first message WAS to the poor and downcast ,unless it endeavoured to uplift them and make their lives brighter and happier' it had altogether failed to carry out the principles of its great Founder. Mr. Matthews had done a great w irk in , Warrington nobly and wall, but there was a : greater and broader field in Sheffield where they were sure he wauld do justice to his position and to the faith he professed. (Applause.) I The Rev. J. S. HUGHES said they all admired and loved Mr. Matthews. W trrington was doing itself I honour by recognising the worth of the services of a good citizen and no one could deny that Mr. Matthews had contributad by his energy, time and talents to the development and uplifting of the paople of Warrington. Many of the young men esoocially would for a long I time bless the day th it Mr. Matthews came to the I town. His character had been transparently beautiful. His nature was full of sympathy, and his soul had been passionate in the yearning for good work. He had been a devoted pastor, a diligent student, an able scholar, a fearless reformer, and a true friend. No church could have been better serv.-d or have had a more ideal pastor Ithan the Latchford Baptist Church and Warrington had need of fearless and strong men like Mr. Matthews. (Applause). Mr. C. H. HEATON DRAPPLE, of Sheffield, said they • recognized Mr. Matthews' gifts when he visited them 1 and they were looking for great things from his ministry.

Mr. 'lames BALL, as representing the Independent Labour Party, said that Mr. Matthews had not forgotten during the whole of the time he bad been in Warring- ton that in addition to being a minister be was also a man and a citizen, and they had been gratified to find that he bad taken a very keen interest in local affairs and national politics and in the methods of the recon- struction of our social and individual order which he thought required placing on a new and more just basis. (Applause.) The members of the Independent Labour Party had been pleased to have Mr. Matthews' assist- ance on many occasions. The most valuable work he had done for them had been to take a class of young men and endeavour to see that their democratic and possibly revolutionary ideas were based upon know- ledge and not upon mere sentiment or any wild sense of injustice. He (Mr. Ball) was convinced that Mr. Matthews' work in Sheffield would be a crown and glory to biro. He had no Leodicean attributes in his character but his utterances were fall of force, vigour and directness. (Applause). Mr. WILLIAM ROBMITS, in making the presentation,- said the great mass of the members of the Free Churches greatly appreciated the work Mr. Matthew had done since he came to Warrington. He had some- times gone about hatlfss, but he was never friendless (Laughter and applause.) The presence of so many young men and women was a splendid proof of the value of the friendship shown to them by Mr. Matthews and he (Mr. Roberts) believed the secret of much of his power was that when he met a working man in the street, no matter bow black his face and hands might be, he had not been above stopping and talking to him.- (Applause.) He (Mr. Roberts) had not agreed with Mr. Matthews many a time, but he had never ceased to respect him. Warrington needed strong, vigorous, enthusiastic men like Mi Matthews, and he (Mr. Roberts) had particularly admired his loyal devotion to the cause which was very near his heart—the cause of temperance. (Applause.) He had often wondered at the amount of work Mr. Matthews had been able to accomplish; he was always a man in a hurry. (Leughter and applause.) Afr. Roberts referred to the willingnesg with which people of all shades of opinion had sub- subscribed to the testimonial fund, whieh bad been quite a voluntary matter, and concluded by handing Matthews a purse containing Z 25. (Applause.) The Rev. ,J. F. Marrnew's in reply said it scarcely seemed possible that such a gathering should take place in connection with his career, and he had been wondering whether he was in a dream and ,what the waking would be like. As he told his own people that morning, he thought it possible for a great deal of esteem and regard to grow up between a minister and his congregation, but he had not believed until very recently that anything like real and abiding affection' could become so warm and tender as that which had united him to his people at Letchford, much less that 'an outside public, however much they might appreciate a man's services, would venture to care for him at all. He was more than grateful for their kindness,syrnpathy and regard. Continuing Mr. Matthews spoke of the invaluable help his wife bad given him in his work and said his greatest joy was to feel that she was proud and pleased that such an occasion as that should have happened in the history of her husband. He had tried to go about his work and he bad net cared two pence what people thought about him. He bad tried to sa7 the right thing and he knew be had been right- (Laughter and applause.) If in doing what he was con- vinced was right be had offended, he asked them of their charity to forgive him. If ha, in the doing of it, had done some good,then if his was the honour, His was the glory and theirs and his the mutual benefit. (Applause.) He was glad to think that as he left the dear old town be carried with bins innumerable marks of friendship and esteem ; and the regard of the young men was very precious to him. Ha hoped in his new ministry to achieve some measure of success, that Sheffield would be pleased to recog- nise his work as a minister in their midst by loyalty one catholicity of regard to him, and that they in Warrington would be prouder in the days to come of the minister who had laboured amongst them than they were even that night. (Applause). The Rev. JOHN YONGE having pronounced the Bene- diction, the meeting concluded.

So diFtressing are the plain facts of the history of Mr.' A. B. BURFORD, of Rochester, that only •brief reference to the details is possible in this -Bpace. The unfortunate young man, while fol- lowing trade as a fitter, happened to hit his leg againbt some metal ; from that trivial wound such calamities developed that he was reduced to clespair. Fir,t, blood plisouing sat in and for -six weeks he Play helpless in bed under medical treatment. Still the mischief spread and after removal to hospital one of his legs had to be a, napntated. This appeared to be the climax of m Woes, but the worse trials Mr. Burford had to face were yet unknown to him.

div.head: FORLORN CASE.
div.p: A FORLORN CASE.

After be had rallied sufficiently some time was R pent at a convalescent institution, but when later he returned to his home at 160, Delco Road, Rochester, it was evident that the mischief was risi)t arrested, for abscesses began to form all over h!a body and he became so painfully weak that 18 friends felt sure he must die under these afflictions. To continue the account from this stage in Air. Burford's own words:

"Everything possible was done for me" he stated, "yet the blood poisoning and the terrible abscesses seemed to be hurrying we to the brink of the grave. I was unable to d ) anything for Week and my mother nursed me day an.i night. Week followed week, but treatment was all to n) purpo,e.

" A-s you see by the remaining scars, the abscesses covered my legs, arms, chest, and bead, and drained my system of every atom of strength . and I was further enfeebled by not being able to retain the lightest solid food.

div.head: WEAK A.ND DELIRIOIB WITH PAIN.
div.p: WEAK A.ND DELIRIOIB WITH PAIN.

"The abscesses made rapid headway, and I was then told that nothing could cure me. I had to keep to my bed, prostrate with weakness, and frequently d•slirious with pain. " In spite of treatment the blood poisoning nad infected my whole system, and the abscesses were eating into my bones. Medical men told my mother that it was only a qnestion of time, and that I should not live very long. Altogether I must have had 15 or 16 doctors attending me for myillness,but all agreed that I could not recover. "In my desplir I turned to other remedies, but nothing did me the slightest good. Then an old lady who knew of my state, called and

advised my parents to give me a steady course of Dr. Williams Pink Pills, which, from her know- ledge, she said, had worked some marvellous cures. My parents had long abandoned all hope of my recovery ; however, they obtained a supply of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills' they rue, and I took them regularly.

div.p: ADDRESS BY TIIE INSI'KCTOR.

Mr. LOWRY then addressed the meeting. With regard to the proposed extension he said he was glad the Board bad recognized that the time had come when they could no longer defer making increased provision for the numbers who came into the House. He noticed that morning that there seemed to he a kind of idea that the Guardians had not made up their minds on the point, but he hoped that simply meant that they had not finally committed themselves and not that they were in a state of hesitation about it, There was nothing in ' the Board's letter specially relating to the ‘Varrington Union. It was simply carrying out the practice adopted three or four years ago of requiring that thestinal estimate , submitted to the Local Government Board should be based on real facts. Mr. Lowry paid a tribute to the great work of the late Sir J. I'. Hibbert and said it was merely from a sense of duty that the Board refused to sanction the proposed expenditure on a memorial. That was the last time he would meet the B rard before the report of the Royal Commission on the Poor Ltw Was received.He hoped,notwithetanding anything there mihgt be in the report, for many more opportunities of meeting them. Mr. Fortstiaw asked if the Inspector thought in view of the effect of old age peusions and of the forthcoming, report of the Royal Commission, the proposed exten- sion scheme ought to go on. The rates were very high at present. Mr. LOWRY said be wag certainly of opinion that the extension was necessary and he did not think the effect of the Old Age Pensions Act or of any legislation which might result from the report of the Royal Corn. mission, was likely to reduae the pressure upon the indoor accommodation. Mr. FORSHAW : Old Age Pensions would be likely to do so. Mr. LOWRY : That is a matter of opinion. Mrs. SIMPSON said it seemed to her that in a few years the pensions would have the effect of diminish- ing the number of old people in the Workhouse. Miss BROAD BENT : They will increase the number. r The CHAIRMAN thought that notwithstanding the pensions many people would be obliged to come into the proposed infirm block, as ss. per week would not keep them outside, Mr. LOWRY was warmly thanked for his address.

div.p: Iff/ARRIMGTON
HEM PETIIM
CHARGES OF BRIBERY AND TREATING.
Mr. Dickens, K.O , Opens the Case.
PENKETH.

Surctim AT PExturrir.—Nluch consternation and I regret was caused in the village of Penketh on Thurs- day afternoon last week when the news was circulated that a well-known villager Mr. George Fone, of Doe Green, had committed suicide by hanging himself in the next door neighbour's hen run. The inquest was held at the Crown and Cushion Inn on Saturday morn- ing by Coroner Brighouse.—Ann Fone, wife of the deceased, said he was GI years of age last October. Ho was a tanner by trade and had been employed up to 11 weeks ago at the Penketh tannery. In the latter part of last year deceased fell down some stone steps at the tannery and had been under the doctor's care for 10 weeks, lie had not worked since the accident. On the 27th of last month deceased told her " that he would not be able to work any more." On the Thurs- day afternoon she saw him walking in the garden. Deceased had never "looked up" since he met with the accident ; he had not been the same man.—Ellen Carman a neat door neighbour, said that about three o'clock on the Thursday afternoon, she went out into the garden and found the deceased hanging by his neck to the top of the fowl run. She summoned her husband wfa) was working close by and he cut deceased down.—Joseph Carman, husband of the last witness, said that when found, deceased had a piece of rope round his neck and he was in a kneeling position. Deceased could have saved himself if he desired, by standing up erect, as it was he had strangled himself. %Vitness justslipped back the knot on the rope and the deceased was free. After discussion in co ivate the jury returned a verdict of "suicide whilst of unsound mind." The coroner expressing sympathy with the wife and son of the deceased.—Deceased will be much missed in the village. He was a highly respected man and up to the time of his death was n member of the Bible Class conducted by Mr. C. E. Parker at the Wesleyan Church.

The astonishing statement that Asthma can be cured, coming from so well-known authority as Dr. Rudolph Schiffinan, wll be of interest to asthma sufferers. The experience of most Asthmatics has been that little if any relief has been afforded them by the methods heretofore employed, and, in fact, the disease has up to now been regarded as incurable. This noted physician has, however, after a life-long study of Asthma and kindred diseases, discovered a remedy which not only instantly relieves the severest cases of Asthma and Bronchitis, but has actually cured thousands whose cases had been pronounced incurable. So complete is Dr. Schiffmann's confidence in his remedy that he requests this paper to announce that he offers to send a liberal sample package of" S2hiffnaann's Asthma Cure" free of charge-to all persons who will send him their name and address, plitinly written on a post-card, within the next 4 days. Ile believes that an actual test will be the most con- vincing, and in fact the only way to overcome the natural prejudice of thousands of Asthmatics who have heretofore sought relief in vain. Alth nigh most chemists in Oreat.Britain have sold his Asthma Cure ever since it was introduced to the British public, still the Doctor fears there are some persons who have never heard of it, and it is with a view to reach- ing these that he makes this liberal offer. An opportunity to test, without cost, a remedy so celebrated and promising so much certainly should be eagerly grasped by every sufferer. . Address Dr. R. div.head: LIVBRPOOL.
div.p: LIVBRPOOL.
THE EXAMINER
FEBRUARY 6th. 1909.
We must apologise both to
THE CON- the " Ddily News" and to SCRIPTION CALL. some of our friends of the

National Service League for importing the above headline. The Leaguers hate to be labelled " conscriptionists " for the simple reason that conscription is thoroughly well hated all the world over and would not be tolerated for a moment in this country. What the National Service League offers for borne consumption is a sweet-coated pill guaranteed to improve the physique and morale of the race. Tne chief ingredients are compulsory military training for all youths between the ages of 18 and 21 for four months in the first year, and a musketry training and a fortnight in camp for the next three years. The germs of conscription may be hidden away, but they are not concealed, and we contend that it is only fair to assume the gradiud growth of national service or compulsory training into the exict equivalent of continental conscription. The National Service League is very active and Insistent on pushing its propaganda down the public throat, and it cannot either escape or reasonably resent criticism. This week the League has issued a manifesto which proposes to engraft compulsory training upon Mr. Haldane's Terri- torial Army scheme. The manifesto is signed by Lord Roberts as President, the Duke of Welling ton, the Rai of Meath, Viscount Milder, Lord Curzon and Lord Riglan, vice-presidents. It refers somewhat patronisingly to Mr. Haldane's scheme, which is described as being excellent as a basis of organisation for home defence, but has some fatal defects ascribed to its voluntary character. The "Daily News" devotes a some- what scathing leading article to the manifesto in which it says : "To begin with, it is really absurd for these irresponsible gsntlemen to issue a letter to the Press declaring that conscription, as advocated by them, wlll cost only four millions a year. The official estimate, presented to both Houses of Parliament by no less a person, we believe, than Mr. Arnold Forster himself, puts the figure at twenty millions, or five times the amount. . . . . We need only remark, in conclusion, that the real inwardness of the movement towards compulsory military service is not, and never has been, defence. These Mandarins want to dragoon a progressive democracy to their will."

The " Westminster Gszstte " protests against the purpose of the League just as strongly lout in more restrained laLguage. This joarn4l, which is respected everywhere for its clear-sightedness ao d temperate judgment of public affairs, gives the Leaguers credit for sincerely believing that the country is in danger, but adds : " We will not enter again into the controversy about compulsory service, except just to say that we profoundly mistrust all calculations which suggest to us that it can be a little thing or a cheap thing. If invasion is a serious danger, it must be a great thing on the Continental model; if it is not a serious danger, and if the strategists are right in not asking us to contemplate more than a raid, then our Territorial Force on a voluntary basis is the right way to meet it. It is right because the alternative of compulsory service raises enormous practical difficulties in the recruiting of the Regular Army and threatens us with expenditure which, at its lowest, must be a serious rival to the necessary expenditure on the Navy. Also because our national policy does not or ought not to require the kind of army pro- posed to us. The voluntary army is our proper ideal, and service in it should be regarded as a privilege and a distinction."

No doubt many of our readers will have read Mr. Townroe's articles on compulsory training, which conclude in to-day's issue. We have willingly given space for the advocacy of the National Service League proposals, not from any feeling of sympathy, but because we consider the question is one which should be considered in all its bearings. Mr. Townroe invited criticism, and we are glad to be able to assure him of a categorical reply to his contentions. Next week we shall commence a series of articles which will paint the other side of the picture. They will be written by Mr. Harold Gray, a young Warrington man of progressive though', and high ideals.

The Conservative Party is THE in the unhappy condition of 'UNHAPPY FAMILY. the man who, exasperated by bickering and dissension in the bosom of his family, vents his ill-temper on the slightest provocation upon any one who thwarts him in the least in the course of his business. That, surely, must be the explanation of the grotesque extravagance with which Opposi- tion speakers are flinging the most ludicrous accu- sations against the Government. Conscious of being no longer united by a common policy and a common creed, they are snatching at such a phantom of unity as Sir

Edward Carson has urged h's Party to pursue by the suggestion that they had at least a common enemy whom they desired to destory. They are attempting to drown the tumult of their own quarrels by the noisy clamour with which they denounce the Government. If it were not for this,the most rudimentary sense of humour would have restrained some of their latest explosions. The Government is raining Chnstianity ; it is responsible for the Tottenham murders; it has blocked land purchase in order to ferment agrarian crime in Ireland ! To such desperate straits has the Opposition been reduced, not only by a fundamental division upon the proplsal to tax the necessaries of life, but by the failure to evolve any settled and consistent programme on the part even of those who are fanatical converts to the antiquated creed of Protection.

subject to confirmation at LIE BRIDGE INN the adjourned Sessions on LICENCE. March 5.,h ricxt, the licence of the Bridge Inn was yesterday transferred to the new Orford lintel to he erected in Gorsey-lane. After the Licensing Committee had been enlarged so as to include the whole 13tich wetz anticipated such a result. The moral objections to the exploiting of a new residential district by the brewers are as strong to-day as they were when the transfer was ref osed a year ago, but the full Bench has proved more susceptible to the voice of the charmer than the special L;censing Committee. The Warrington Bridge scheme seems to have turned the scale, and once again it has to be deplored that under such circumstances as these, public improvements are liable to blind public men to the sacred trust they hold for the preservation of public morality. We shall discuss the merits and demerits of the bargain more fully next week.

The reverend gentleman THE Ray. J. F. who has just said farewell MATTHEWS. to Warrington after eleven and a half years in our midst has heard so many valedictory addresses , during the last few ddys that he will doubtless be able to bear with us patiently while we add one more testimony to the service he has rendered to the community in general as well as to his own church. Mr. Matthews came to Warrington a young man with faith, ideals, energy and earnest- ness, and he leaves the town to-day even better eqnipped for the work before him. He is still a young man, his faith has been tempered and strengthened by the fires of experience and adversity, and the ideals of twelve years ago are still the ideals which will lead him on and on till his life's work is done. Mr. Matthews has never forsaken his ideals or allowed them for one moment to get out of reach. We doubt not they will seem as near, as radiant, and as inspiring in Sheffield as in Wirrington. He has always been fitted for a larger sphere than was allotted him in Warrington, though even here Mr. Matthews often measured his circle of activity solely by the standard of his capacity, and not by circumstances. He might have vegetated in Latchford, but he always had the spirit to do and dare, and we believe it will be one of Mr. Matthews' most cherished recollections that his life in Warrington was productive of a many-sided service which bore good fruit and earned the approbation mad gratitude of a wide community.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

The Earl of Ranfurly, whose eldest son, Viscount Northland, is co-defendant in the Stirling divorce case now at hearing in Edinburgh, is the head of the Knox family, and claims a common ancestor with the famous John Knox, of the Scottish ReCormation period. Lord Guthrie, who is trying the case, is the author of an admirable biography of John Knox, and the editor of Knox's own history of the Scotch Reformation. * * *

As a rule the business of the Fire Engine Com- mittce does not excite much attention at meetings of the Town Council. On Tuesday Alderman Burton insisted on laying emphasis on various items in the Superintendent's annual report, and if he did not always claim the serious attention of his audience he contrived to amuse them at times. For instance in moving the minutes, the Alderman said solemnly : " Work is going on satisfactorily as usual, we had four fires last month." It seems quite certain that if there there were no fires necessitating the attention of the brigade, the members of the Committee would be walking about with long faces deploring the hard times and lack of business. We wonder if Tariff Reform would find work for unemployed fire brigades.

The report of the Superintendent of the Fire Brigade discloses some interesting facts. The damage resulting from fires in the borough during the year was only 5,4,101, as compared with £20,501, in the previous year. Of the 33 fires attended,seven were at farms, which easily hold the record for com- bustibility. Stables, which are somewhat akin to farms, come next with three fires. Only two cottages needed the help of the fire-fighters, which. caused Alderman Burton to pass a eulogy on the care of the Warrington cottagers. Considering the enormous difference in the numbers of each, it seems odd to find as many milliners' shops and wire works in the list as cottages, i.e. two. Only one newspaper office has been on fire, and this outbreak was attributed (by Alderman Tinniou) to the " dryness " of the newspapers produced. The Brigade received nearly twice as many calls at night as in the day-time.

Felix Mendelssohn-Bartholdy whose centenary was celebrated on Wednesday is best known to the man- in-the•street as the composer of the great oratorios of " Elijah" and " St. Paul," and by his famous "Songs without Words." Lie was a native of Hamburg, and was the son of a wealthy Jew, who recognising his son's talent at an early age, had him specially trained. Mendelssohn was only sixteen years old when he pro- duced the well-known overture to the "Midsummer Night's Dream." He was musical director to the King of Saxony, and was very frequently in this country, where he used to conduct his own works. Mendelssohn died at a very early age, for he was only thirty eight when he passed away at Leipzig. * *

Modern conditions (says Country Life" seem about to drive the last remnant of the rambling folk who pass generally by the name of gipsies into town life. In the first place there is the Children's Act. After it comes into operation the little barbarians will have to be educated and taken care of just as if they belonged to cities. It will be no easy task at the beginning; those imps of the open air by their very look proclaim that they are more like wild creatures than human children. They have been taught to beg, and are clever in a" doggy ' kind of way, but real intellect has never been stirred in them. If the schoolmaster succeeds in doing so, be will have given the finishing blow to the "ganging folk," as they are called in Scotland.

* * * We have all met at some time or another the clever man who can tell us much more about ourselves than we had ever dreamed of. Lord Robert Cecil has no small share of this kind of cleverness. He says that " the present Government went to the electors with intimation that they had a sovereign remedy for unemployment." This is a wonderful revelation. We had always thought that the Tariff Reformers possessed the monopoly of these sovereign remedies. Mr. Austen Chamberlain, speaking at the annual dinner of the Birmingham Jewellers and Silversmiths' Association, referred to a numbers of remedies for unemployment" suggested or supported by his political opponents." Technical education, labour exchanges, reorganization of work in periods of depression, so that instead of some men being discharged all should work short time—these proposals were passed in review, and contemptuously dismissed as mere palliatives. No, it is the Tariff Reformers who claim to have the sovereign remedy for unemployment. But is it really worth a sovereign? • Wycliffe Young People's Society. _ _ _ _ _

Wedding at the Parish Church. Considerable local interest was taken in the wedding which was solemnised at the Parish Church, Warrington, on Wednesday, of Mr. G. llaesmor Harrison, of Grappenhall, son of Mr. G. Harrison, Police Surgeon, Chester, and Miss Laura Helen Ogle Sleigh, daughter of the late Mr. S. H. Sleigh, of Chester. Mr. Harrison is a well-known employe at Pair's Bank, Warrington, and has entered largely into the social life of Grappenhall and district, where he resided. The bride was given away by her cousin, the Rev. Wm. Ogle, and looked very striking in a directoire gown of soft ivory cloth over a vest of tucked net, with bands of soutache braiding. She also wore a white satin hat, with a large bunch of white plumes and a big pearl buckle, and a lace veil. She also carried a bouquet of orange blossom and white roses. tiler sister, Miss Amy Sleigh, was the only bridesmaid and was attired in a grey cloth directoire gown with black hat and white plumes, and carried a boquet of pink roses The bridegroom introduced a somewhat novel feature to a fashionable wedding by appearing at the altar in a purple lounge suit. The Rev. Canon Willis officiated at the ceremony, assisted by the Rev. Hy. Grantham, chap- lain to the forces, Chester, the Revs. T. A. J. Ridpath and T. W. Barber. There were two groomsmen, Mr. Percy Ogle Sleigh and Mr. Max Woods. The service was fully choral and special music was played by the Parish Church Organist, Mr. Darby. At the conclu- sion of the ceremony the bells rang a merry peal. A reception was held later at the Patten Arms Hotel, to which a largo number of well-known people had been invited. The honeymoon is being spent in Salop, at the Lodge, Sambrook, kindly lent by the bride's sister, Mrs. Arthur Jackson. div.head: SERIOUS MOTOR COLLISION.
div.p: SERIOUS MOTOR COLLISION.
A HORSE KILLED AND CART SMASHED.
A Lady Severely Injured.

A sensation was caused in the Latchford district on Saturday evening by a collision between a motor car and a cart on the Knutsford-road, Grappenhall, about 200 yards south of the Latchford Swing Bridge. The car was a big heavy covered vehicle owned by Mr. W. H. Bleckly, of Thelwall (managing director of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, Ltd.), and was in charge of a chauffeur. Mr. Bleckly and his daughter, Mrs. C. Williamson, and her baby and nurse, Miss du Bois were seated in the car when the acccident occurred. The car was coming round a corner when it collided with a horse aud cart owned by Mr. J. B. Isaac, provision dealer, Sankey-street, and in charge of Edward Smith, driver.

The smash was a serious one, the cart being wrecked and the horse so badly injured that it had to be shot immediately. The bonnet of the car forced its way under the horse, and one of the cart shafts crashed through the window of the oar body and struck Miss du Bois in the face, causing serious injuries which neces- sitated her removal to the Infirmary on the horse ambulance. The other occupants of the car most fortunately escaped with nothing worse than a severe shaking. A somewhat remarkable circumstance was that Mrs. Williamson's baby lay on the nurse's knee at the time of her injury, and escaped quite unharmed. The horse which was killed, was valued at £25.

On reaching the Infirmary it was discovered that Uiss du Bois was suffering from severe concussion of the brain and injuries to the jaw. She lay unconscious until Wednesday, but has since made very gratifying progress towards recovery.

div.head: QUESTIONS FOR TARIFF REFORMERS.
div.p: QUESTIONS FOR TARIFF REFORMERS.

XVI.—If "ties of interest" are necessary to make British Colonists love the Empire, how much will the British workman love the Empire when he has to pay more for his bread and meat to make "ties of interest" for the British Colonists P

The " Preference " policy puts the Empire on a cash basis. Not mutual affection, or common language, or common history, or a common civilisation, or ties of blood—not these are to be the nexus of Empire, but "ties of interest" in the shape of "preferences." If such a principle is accepted, why is no "tie of interest" provided for British workmen? Why are they, who so greatly out number British Colonists, to be taxed to make an Imperial bond, and if they are to be taxed, what becomes of the . theory that "tied of interest" are needed?
L. G. C. IL

div.head: TARIFF REFORM DEBATE CHALLENGE.
div.p: THE TARIFF REFORM DEBATE CHALLENGE.
Progrtssive Labour League's Reply.

We have received the following copy of a letter from the Secretaries of the Progressive Labour League, which has been addressed to the Tariff Reform League, local branch, with regard to the proposed public debate on Tariff Reform.

Warrington, February 2nd, 1909. Dear sirs,—We are sorry you appear to hare mis- understood our last letter. If you will kindly look at it again you will see that what we desired was to bring about a set Public Debate between two representative men. Such a discussion ai you suggest is now taking place at the local Parliamentary Debating Society and therefore need not be repeated. We are desirious that you should put forward the most able man you can find in the country, and we are prepared to find an opponent to meet him so that we may have a thoroughly representative meeting likely to interest the town and do justice to both sides of this question. If your Society will agree to this suggestion, arrangements can be made at once.
- Yours faithfully, . J MORTON, Hon. Secretsties. J. HOWES, Jun. The Hon. Secretaries, Tariff Reform League, Warrington.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL FESTIVAL. – Last Night's Local Contests.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL FESTIVAL. - Last Night's Local Contests.

The Warrington Musical Festival made a successful start last evening with a programme entirely devoted o local contests. There was a good attendance at the Parr Hall and the various events were followed with keen interest and not a little enthusiasm. Admirable arrangements have been made by a strong and repre- sentative committee under the chairmanship of Mr. E. Lloyd Jones with Mr. IL W. Cook as hon. secretary. The services of two eminent adjudicators—Mr. S. Coleridge-Taylor and Mr. Harry Evans—have been obtained and everything points to the present festival being a complete success in every respect. The Deputy- Mayor (Alderman J. Smethurst) presided at last night's gathering and warmly commended the festival and encouraged its promoters in their work on behalf of musical culture. div.head: BOXING AT THE BARRACKS.
div.p: BOXING AT THE BARRACKS.

People interested in the noble art of self-defence have been afforded an excellent opportunity of witness- ing some splendid Boxing this week at the Orford Barracks. The contests were open to all troops in the . . .

Western Command, Regulars,' Special Reserve and Territorials.—The tournament opened on Thursday night before a large audience. A splendid and com- modious ring had been provided for the competitors. The chief event of the evening was the 18 round contest betwqen two Warrington lads in the persons of George Warren and Jimmy England. The first three rounds were spent in discoveringeach other's tactics but at the end of the fourth t ound England brought his opponent to the floor by a blow on the side of the head. Warren regained his feet just before the time-keeper recorded time. The sth and 6th rounds were spent in repeated blows from each side, England's left arm frequently reaching his opponent's face. In the 11th round England got in two or three staggering blows about the face and body of his opponent who stuck to his post pluckily, and by deft arm work stopped many blows which, had they gone home, would steadily have ended the match. In the last rolls(' both opponents went in the fray desper- ately, but neither succeeded in administering the knock- out blow. The referee, Mr. Joe Pollitt, of the "Sportsman," proclaimed England the winner by points amid tremendous applause from the audience. On the last occasion when these two competitors met, the contest was given a draw. The last match was fought with 6-oz. gloves and two minutes rounds. Great interest!was centered in the eight round con- test between Lance-Corporal Tavlin and Jonty Hayward the former of the 2nd South Lancashire Regiment-, Buttevant, and the latter of Salford. In the third round the corporal twice brought his opponent to the boards by terrific body blows but he pluckily resumed. In the latter part of the match Hayward was having the best of the contest, and at the conclusion of the Bth round he was proclaimed the winner on points. Other matches were r(recruits 10 stone and under) Private Harrison, of the Cheshire Regiment, beat Private Dixon ; Private Rayner boat Private Drescoll; Private Bate beat Private Brennan. In the contest for N.C.O.'s and trained men, Private Lay beat Private Taylor; Private Connor beat Sergeant Calverts ; and Private Ryan beat Corporal Gatenby.

div.head: MR. RAMSAY MACDONALD, M.P.
div.p: MR. RAMSAY MACDONALD, M.P.

Photo, London News Agency, Ltd. Mr. J. R.k/ISAY MACDoNALD, M.P., began his speech With a reference to the Labour Party's recent confer- ence at Portsmouth. Before that conference, it was predicted that party t the there was going to be split, that was going to be a great earthquake similar, in P—"cs, to the one that visited Italy the other day, and that those who had been building up 'the great labour movement were to leave Portsmouth killed Politically and with their movement shattered about their ears. The earthquake, however, not come off ; the political murders did not happen; Portstnouth instead of shattering the movement had eonsolidated it, and insteatrof showing that the move- " Meat was split had shown that it was united with a more intense desire for union than ever had been sPparent before. Tne movement was larger, better- organized, more coherent than ever. He believed 'everybody admitted that the coming session of Parlia- ment was going to bc a very critical one not merely for the Government but for the country. We were entering a new time of politics altogether. The days When politics were the recreations of the declining years of the rich were over and the time had come for politics to be the serious study of the youthful years of all classes, rich and poor alike. The State was no longer merely the provider of the policeman and the battleship; it was the custodian of the conditions in which -the moral nature of man could develop. That opened an enormously wide field. They were bringing politics -down to the hearthstones of the people. There was not a Single problem, from the general national problem ,vottmemployment to the personal problem such as that vdtTh waa now being unfolded in the Edinburgh Courts --hut 84:4;i Incla disgusting disgrace to society—(upplanse) >of the Statvra'2l,4ow being associated with the duty -or -- and with the fact that the State as an gSvnised whole had failed to do its duty to the di idual and to society. There were two great questions that must be faced—unemployment and la_ational finance—and the two could not be separated lEnnl each other. Unemployment was not the expres- sion of individual shortcoming at all. So long as the Present system of society lasted, with the land and 'Capital monopolised by a few, we were absolutely bound to face periods of unemployment every, now and again. Modern society required unemployed. At the very best it never could employ more than 97A to 98 per cent of lhe men asking for work. In that case he contended 'that modern society ought to look after the unemployed. (Applause.) He was beginning to think the Govern- neeat was not going to fulfil this year the promise it made as year. year. The Government told them it WAS not pre - Pared to deal with the unemployed question until it 'received the report of the Poor Law Commission. In his life he (the speaker) liked to be reasonable. t looked very well sometimes to put up a great fight irrespective of the rationality of their Position but his heart was never in such fights, and he as bound to say that if the Government had put the `:Unemployed Workmen's Act into fulToperation and said You really cannot reasonably expect us to produce legislation whilst this commission is sitting " he did (:)t think they could reasonably have expected it—if he Government had shown by its administration that tra was genuine. He was told the report of the Com- hiisssion was not going to be issued until the end of 2month and that it would take the form of a dozen ‘r more large volumes which would require careful :111dY• He said the Government bad deceived them in 'us matter. Ile doubted if the Government would be Prepared to bring in its legislation this year and it would have to take the consequence of repeatedly post- °anbing facing the problem as it ought to be faced. The oar Party's Unemployment Bill held the field and us ventured to say that during the debates upon ti'llil'irnPlnYment it would be found more clearly that the wi the best and most carefully thought out plan, nnth7 its faelts, that had ever been produced to the hi use of Commons for dealing with the problem. Let _passure them categoricolly and definitely that the „"ita_°_o u Party would insist upon a treatment of the "u"mPloyed problem this session, that it would not accept-powr 'n any w order to excuse and that it would use its political entcPel the Government,if the Govern- ment as unwilling, to fulfil the pledges given last year. In saying that, he was not adumbrating heroics. Thirty- one men were but a minority, and if the House did not °erne UP to their expectations the electors themselves responsible, and not the men they Lad sent there ;r1 such small numbers. They were not going to obstruct nosiness, he hoped, because obstruction could be used :verY much more effectively against them than they 'could ese it in their favour. The electors had no business to ask the Labour men to undo by violence the mistakes they made with calmness. (Applause.) At the present time the smart set of society was dividing its attention between the Edinburgh Divorce Court and new play in London. The smart set was that set in EenietY which had all the airs and graces of distinction but all the odours of a very badly kept stable. When he talked or thought of abolishing that set the only Word he could use was that they ought to be drained out of existence. He hated them and if the workers Paid less respect to them and their doinas it would be ii Very lunch better day. (Applause.) Those who had come from the people bad no reason to be ashamed of their origin and they would be betraying their people "less they remembered with pride their origin and stuck to it, and not try to emulate the abominable vices of the better-to-do classes in this country. The PlaY Which theY smart set was going to see did It great many things. It insulted our Volunteer LOrees t it tried to describe by a nonsensical Plot the characters of which were admirable .Snecimens of the stupid upper classes of this country— (ag old man whose brain was muddled ancl young men ho were a disgrace to their class)—A German invasion. awas too- cowardly to say that it W,IS a German lvaSion, but that was what was meant. By that means ?II were trying to get the people of England into a rarn e of mind which-would enable them to accept con- s_eriPtion as the policy of this country. The smart set .nd soldiers like Lord Roberts—about whose soldier- ,:ts___te qualities one had to go to South Africa as he (the ~7nke!) did and find the opinions of the Boer leaders— %llßitt issue thsir manifestoes in order to mislead and .!adireot the tread of political thought and conviction, if the Labour party and the wage-earners were ewiturth their salt they would teach Lord Roberts and his Rotart set and the Navy League that they bad not for- it_leo their political history, that they still valued .4415.2 r English liberties, that they still believed in British irri..._°e!acy, and that they were not going to allow a wiit"lrY system to ride over them either with spurs or V.,0,„"t• (Applause.) At any rate, in the House of of "itons that was the line he would take. Alongside to.d there was a new navy scare. They were told that there was a crisis in the Cabinet. He tee7le th,ere Were men in the Cabinet sufficiently faith oemocratic interests and to the democratic tC that they had been preaching, to refuse 'elnatn. insnde the Cabinet ten minutes after

the big navy league had captured the majority in that Cabinet. The Labour Party, he hoped, would oppose tooth and nail any proposal to threaten Germany by an extra large ship-building programme this year. (Applause.) The class to whom he had been alluding wanted to increase their taxes so that they would sub- mit to their tariff reform parposals. He was going to oppose them in that and he hoped the Labour Party would. They wanted peace and they wanted to be safe from the menace of invasion. There was only one way of securing it and that was by diplomatic means, by an understanding between the great nations of the world. Mr. Macdonald strongly condemned the "miserable. I silly game of beggar-my-neighbour" in the matter of I building war ships. Armaments were not conditions of peace, as superficial observers were so prone to say; they were the preparations and conditions of war, and the time would come when the burdens of England and of Germany would get so great that both the Germans and ourselves would say "Let us fight each other in order to relieve ourselves of the burdens that are accumulating." Every new ship that was laid down made war apparently more and more inevitable and the Admiralties and Foreign Offices and the military and naval staffs got more and. more tightened up in their nerves and more watchful in expectation. Any little scare or misunderstanding between two peoples heavily burndened with armaments, full of suspicions one to another,might simply break the bonds of peace, war would be declared and the wiseacres who quoted the proverb "Armaments are conditions of peace," would then dis- cover when it was too late that armaments brought on a mental tension which precipitated war. The Labour Party's financial proposals were simple and just. Their method was to impose the cost. of Government upon the parasitic class of the community and ease the burdens that had been placed on the backs of capital and labour because the parasitic class had been allowed to go almost scot free. (Applause.) This year, there- fore. the Labour party wanted two things in the Budget—a land tax and a super tax upon large incomes. (Applause.) In conclusion Mr. Macdonald pictured the time when Labour members would be able to say "The people of this country have spoken. We sit no longer in a corner. We sit on the great Benches where the majority sit, and as in the past we destroyed not but increased the respect paid to the House of Commons, which after all is the voice of the people, whether it is the people drunk or the people sober, so now that the instrument is ours, and the weapon is in our hands, we shall use it to widen the outlook of our people, to make their lives purer, happier, and holier, and to make England a great, a mighty, a strong and free Empire." (Applause). The Rev. H. DUNNICO said he used to think Warring- ton was bad enough, but if they wanted to get into a Tory, brewery-ridden city they must go to Liverpool. In an anonymous letter he had been accused of inconsistency in view of the fact that he had previously appeared on a Liverpool platform. Inconsistency was no crime, but was he inconsistent? He had always advocated Socialism in theory. Even when he was inside the Liberal party be was a Socialist, believing in the economics of Socialism, but he bad found out what all sensible men had found out, that Socialism was never coming through either of the preat political parties but only through the Labour Party. (Applause.) He had received a postcard addressed: "Mr. Blatchford,c/o the Rev. H. Dunnico," containing a lot of nonsense about Godless Socialism, the destruction of family life and so on. He was not there to defend Mr. Blatchford, he was quite capable of defending himself. (Applause.) He (the speaker) differed strongly from some of Mr. Blatchford's theological and religious opinions, but he wished to say this : -that if he had to leave this world that night and take his stand before the bar of God, he would rather stand in Robert Blatchford's shoes than in those of the man who wrote that posteard.(Applause.)Dealing with a recent utterance of Mr. Lever on unemployment, Mr. Dunnico said be did not see how any sensible man could say that poverty was due to the fact that we could not produce sufficient necessaries to keep the people in a state of well-being and dinciency. The income of the country amounted to something like .21,750,000,000 or £1,800,000,000 per annum, and if that were equally divided—which they did not advocate—it would provide every family of are people with an income of not less than £2OO per annum. Supposing for the sake of argument that enough was not produeed, we had a simple remedy. It was nonsensical to say that people were starving because we could not produce sufficient when there were hundreds and thousaeds of men willing to work yet compelled to walk the streets. The social problem was a vaster problem than the drink question, although he granted that every social reformer must be a temper- ance reformer. He was, however, afraid that if he had to live and work under the abominable conditions that some men had to, he might get bliud drunk every night. It was the only refuge some peopie had from the grind- ing tyranny and monotony of their every day existence. Poverty was due to unequal distribution of wealth, and he maintained that it would only be overcome by the substitution of a Socialistic State for the present coin- petitice system. The future of the Caristian Church depended upon the attitude it took towards .he great Labour movement.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

The chief attraction this week at the Hippodrome is the big spectacular comedy-drama " Afy pal Jerry„ which takes half-an-hour to present. The story tells. of the trial, sentence, punishment, and escape of Jerry Jackson and Nolabler Nolan, the Bloomsbury burglars, and in rapid sequence the audience is taken through the Central Criminal Court, with judge, jury,- counsel, prisoners and witnesses, the Penton villa Prison, the Portland Quarries, and the scene of the pal's sad parting. Nobbler and Jerry are an uncouth and unprepossessing pair of criminals who give their captors a lively time. Their one redeeming trait of character is their love for one another as pals, which endures even to the.end that Death himself provides. The show is full of mirth and incident, which culminate in tragedy and all the acting is well done. Lew Lake and Bob Aforris particularly distinguish themselves as the burglars, and give a most realistic presentment of the parts they represent. One of the cleverest turns in the bill this week is that of Sergeant Brennan, the champion diaboloist Like Pi ng-po ng, diabolo seemed to have a popular " rage" and then go spark out as a people's game. It is one which, however, possesses infinite p-liSibilities for the individual with skill and aptitude, and Sergeant Brennan's manipulation of the flying spool is nothing less than marvellous. He well earns the heartiest of applause. Mysticus is a performer who well upholds his name in a smart show. If he did nothing else than pull off innumerable pairs of gloves, each one mysteriously succeeded in some invisible way by another pair of different colour, Mysticus would not have appeared in vain. But the glove trick is only one of many which both puzzled and amused. Wilton Heriot and Co. give what is termed a protean comedy sketch "An Anglo-American Alliance.' The male member of the " C )." person- ates five different characters in very quick time, and the lady receives a proposal from each. The sketch is smartly written, original in idea, and well per- formed. Other items in a very full and interesting programme are a display by Kirk and Saraski, the only aquatic acrobats; a song by Adah Payne, who is an excellent soprano vocalist, and a comedy musical act by Captain Ellis and Son, two coloured performers The music and the pictures maintain their high standard of excellence. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

There is another excellent and novel programme for next week, Jake Friedman and powerful cast of 30 star performers will appear in an artistic Dutch operetta "Happy Holland" which is sure to be bright and pleasing. Other attractions will be : —Belle Davis and her Pick Chick Actors ; !Jack Olive in her original whistling scena ; Sable Fern, a singer whose words you can hear; Frank H. Fox, versatile comedian; Clarice Clarke, vocalist.

div.head: WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL TEA MEETING.
div.p: WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL TEA MEETING.

The annual tea meeting in connection with the Wycliffe Congregational Caurch took place on Thurs- day evening in the Memorial buildings. The gathering proved a great success the accommodation of the hall being taxed to the utmost. Palms and decorative material had been used to brighten the appearance of the room. Considerably over 200 people sat down to tea, the tables being waited upon by lady members of the congregation. A brief organ recital was given by Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Rae., the organist and choir- master, which was greatly appreciated. At the subse- quent proceedings the Pastor (the Rev. John Yonge) presided, and in a few introductory remarks said he hoped and trusted that they would have a good year. This was a matter in the hands of the congregation who if they would only work and worship together would make a happy and prosperous church. He cordially welcomed several nea7 friends. A musical programme consisting of vocal and instrumental music, recitations, and a series of delight- ful tableaux vivants arranged by Miss M. Swindells, was submitted. The vocalists were; Miss A. Griffiths, soprano ; Miss M. Hawthorn, contralto ; Mr. A. Griffiths, tenor; Mr. B. Hibbert, bass ; and Messrs. H. Hawthorn, P. O. Bailey, W. Parker, baritanes. All songs were well received and encores wore frequent. A number of ladies of the choir sang the part song "Whispering Wind." The instrumental ists, Mrs. Haviour (violin), Mr. T. R. Ford (concertina), and Masters Knowles and Swain (violin duet) also added to the success of the evening. Recitations by Miss A. Beswick, Miss Corney, and Mr. H. M. Ashton were very aocept- able programme. Mr. W. H. Payton accompanied on the piano with his usual skill. The services of all who had assisted were acknowledged on the proposition of Mr. BOUCHIZItt seconded by Mr. JAMF.s GOULD. An enjoyable evening concluded with the singing of the Doxology. Telco Woods' Great Peppermint Cure, for Coughs and Colds; it never fails. is. lid., 2s. 9d.—Advt.

div.head: LICENSING SESSIONS. -- BRIDGE INN LICENCE TRANSFERRED.
div.p: LICENSING SESSIONS. -- BRIDGE INN LICENCE TRANSFERRED.

The annual licensing sessions for the Borough of Warrington were held at the Police Court yesterday. It had been decided that the whole Bench should con- stitute the Licensing Committee and there was a large attendance of justices. The Mayor (Alderman Forshaw) presided and there were also present :—Aldermen •Smethurst, Tinnion, 113 nnett, Pierpoint and Ellison, Councillor Wilkinson. Dr. For, Dr. Markel, Messrs. John White, John Fairclough, Henry Roberts, W. Roberts, C. S. Burgess, S. Wright, T. Locker, C. Jackson Elolmes, G. Pilling, R. T. Fairclough, A. J. Jolley, H. Thornton, W. Richardson, J. W. Hayward, and E. J. Guest. TIE CLIIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT.

The Chief Constable reported that the number of licence holders in the Borough was 198, a decrease of three upon last year, caused by the refusal of the Bench to renew three off-licences. There were 13 less licences now in the Borough as compared with 1898. The population of the Borough according to the census of 1901 was 64,242, consequently there existed (on these figures) in Warrington one licensed house to every 324-42 inhabitants. With reference to the drunkenness, there was a decrease of twenty-two in the number of, persons proceeded against as compared with the pre- vious year. Of the 308 persons proceeded against 213 were residents of the Borough, and 95 strangers to the town. There was a decrease in the number of residents prosecuted for drunkenness during the yeAr as com- pared with the figures of the previous twelve months, when there was also a satisfactory decrease as compared with 1906. (A table giving the days of the week on which drunkenness occurred showed that Saturday easily headed the list). A largo number of surprise visits of inspection were made by the police to licensed premises during the twelve months with a result that on a few occasions the attention of the Licensees had to be drawn to slight irregularities, but on the whole the houses app3ared to have been satis- factorily oonductel.
