div.head: TffE BRIDGS INN.
div.p: TffE BRIDGS INN.

Lamm TRANSPEEMED TJ GDR 3ET-LANE. Mr. Browne said he wts instructed to apply on behalf of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and C in the name of Mr. Henry Ashton, for the provisional removal of the Hoene() of the Bridge Inn to a house known as the Orford Hotel, to be erected at the corner of Gorsey- lane and Norris-street. H 3 referred to the plicy inaugurated in 1892 at the suggestion of Mr. Frederick Monks, then chairman of the Licensing Committee, whereby houses in congested areas had been reduced and others built in outlying districts. Tne result was that since 1832 the number of fully-licensed houses in the town had been reduced from 87 to 82 and the beer- house licences from 43 to 36. Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Ca. had met the Bench lea handsome way by putting up good buildings, reducing congestion in the centre of the town, and in addition they had rebuilt a number of houses by order of the Bench, under the 193 t Act* With regard to the present application there was no doubt that a new Warrington Bridge must be built— whether it was ferro-concreto or steel was a question for the Corporation. The new bridge, whether it was 60 feet or 89 feet wide—he hoped it would be 80 feet— must cause the Bridge Inn te be pulled down. Whether they said Messrs. Fairclough on the other side must pulled down or not, the Bridge Inn must come down to do away with the curve. From the Lower Seven Stars to the Packet House Inn and to the line of the bridge Itself was a parallel line, and he therefore contended that the widening must be on the other side and to obviate the shocking curve to get round to Wilierspool Causeway the Bridge Inn would have to be demolished. In asking for the removal of the licence his clients were not giving up any trivial matter. Lie Bridge Inn was a very good house, doing a substantial business, ant kept by one of the bast known members of the Northern League of football. It was therefore not with the idea that it was a poor house that the application was made. Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Ca., were ratepayers like everybody else. Tney had their trallic from Wilderspool Brewery over the Warrington Bridge to consider, and it was to their interests that a new bridge should be built. In order to help the town they pro- posed to ask the Bench to remove the licence to a house to be built at Orford. By doing so they would remove a great eye sore in the shape of the stable buildings, &c., and they would be helping on the work of the Beautiful Warrington Society. With regard to the Orfoid neighbourhood, since the application was made last year 211 new houses had been built and the whole of the plot of land snrrounding the neighbourhood of the site had been let for building purposes and in a few years time would be absolutely filled with property. lie had a number of most rasa-actable witnesses who would tell the Bench that at present they could not conveniently satisfy their re isoaable requirements. The Cemetery Inn was 745 yards away; William Price's off-licence in Orford-lane, 903 yards; Joseph Whit- field's off-licence in Battersby-lane, 94 yards ; King ' and Queen, Padgate-lane' 1,004 yards; Albion H net Bettersby-lane, 1,045 yards; off-licence in Manchester- , road, 1,078 yards. The licensed houses in iNarrington worked out at one to every 353 inhabitants—one of the best averages of anftown in Lancashire—and he thought that. was due to the readiness of Messrs. Greenall Whitley and Co. to meet the suegeetions of the Hooch in regard to congested- areas. For the Orford district, taking a half-mile radius, the licenees worked out at one to 1612 inhabitants, and he therefore submitted that an additional house was certainly necessary. He asked the Bench to look ahead and not to be purblind in the matter. They all knew, if their forefathers had only looked beyond their noses, what a great expense would have been saved in Bridge-street and other places. In giving up the Bridge Inn the firm also handed over the land and buildings, the area of which was 562 square yards (exclusive of the cottage which was not their property) absolutely free to the Corporation for the purposes of the improvement and in addition, when the final grant of the licence was made, they would close, without compensation, the Little Horse Shoe, Horse- market-street,which was doing an excellent lonsiness,had good stabling accommodation, and might be worth anything up to £4,00) or £5,000. In reply to the Bench, Mr. Browne said the firm would in all probability arrange for the stah'es to be added .to the Blue Bell, as they were a benefit to the town.

_ The Mayor : Is the new house to be built on the same site as was proposed last yeti-? The Clerk: It is exactly the same, except .that Norris-street is completed. Mr. Henry Ashton was called and formally made the application. Aiderman Tinnion : Is it your intention to live at the house when it is built? Mr. Ashton: Yes.

_ Alderman Tinnion : For any length of time? Mr. Ashton: I cannot sly any particular period, but I shall stay there for a length of time. Evidence in support of the application was given by Mr. Afarshall, 48, Norris-street, foreman porter in the employ of the Cheshire Linea Committee, Alfred

Holloway, wiredrawer, 28, Norrls-street, and Alfred Fryer, engine-driver, 59, Wilkinson-street. The last- named witness said he had not heard the slightest objection raised in the neighbourhood to the proposed new houde.

Mr. Browne intimated that he had five other witnesses but it was not considered necessary to call them. There was no opposition. After the Bench had deliberated in private,the Mayor said the application would be granted on the conditions stated with the addition that an off-licence in Brick- street should also be surrended.
Mr. Browne intimated his client's willingness to comply with this request. The decision will come up for confirmation at the adjourned Sessions on March sth.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. By "
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. By "

It was a disappointment to Warrington people to learn on Saturday evening that the W.irepullers hal failed to win at Wakedeleby the narrow margin of a try to nil. They had such: a strong side in the field that they were quite expected to beat the Trinitarians for the second time this season. Under some circum- stances they might have done so, but on Saturday they could do no better than gi,re Wakefield a very warm and exciting 80 minutes. This was only the second occasion during the season that Warrington have been nilled, the first being at Hull, so that the other side of the Pennine Chain cannot be considered a happy hunting ground for the Wirepullers.

Wakefield harl their full team available for the i first time since the New Year, and their supporters were quite confident of a comfortable victory by 15 clear points. As a muter of foci th, Trinity were somewhat lucky to get the only try of the match, for the scorer was actually pulled over the line by a reck- less Warrington forward who joined Treharne in the tackle. Warrington were every bit as gaol as their oppments, and combined* rather more effectively in mid-field', but those essentials which lea], to succes, were missing. Why? Because the ground was really unfit for play.

I have never seen a Rugby match played oa harder ground. It was m3re like a cement pavement sprinkled over w:th dead grass thaa anything else. The little pools ro Ind th 3 edges of the field were all ice, and there had not, apparently,: been any thaw since the early morning frost. Even to take a goal-kick players could make no heel mark in the stony turf, and it was no wonder that the men did not give of their best under such conditions. Wakefield seemed determined to win,and by.reckless,lf not deliberately foul,tacklin,g they laid out three of Warrington's best backs —Fish, Dickenson, and Brooks—in/the first twenty minutes. Bennett deserved marching orders for the "tackle " which brought Fish down. It was nothing more or leas than a swinging blow across the face wheri travelling at full speed. Dickenson was treated in the same way, and the Wakefield "tackle" will not be forgotten in a moment.

These pleasant incidents, coupled with the hard around, naturally made the Warrington men cautious of their bones. There was none of that breaking through by Brooks, after the first attempt, and one cannot blame him. The centres were also warned by experience whit to expect, and the result wafts a lot of passing of the ortholox description which generally ended in touch. Wakefield playei desperately; and it says something for Warrington's tactics that there was not a single Wakefield man hurt throughout the match.

On soft turf I feel sure the r3sutt wotxld have been reversed. Warrington had a superior side, and that extra bit of cleverness would have pulled them through if the conditions had been fit for the game.MWakefield were a good, level lot, and particularly fast forward, but the backs did not impress one with individual greatness. Bennett was the worst and Metcalfe the best. The veteran full back fielded and panted beautifully, while Tilley- was only inferior in the length of his kicking. There was no waiting for a bouncing ball on Saturday, as the oval frequently bounded 30 feet high on the hard ground.

Candidly speaking I was not favourably impressed with the sportsmanship of the Wakefield men either inside or outside the playing area. The spectators could see nothing creditable in the best of Warrington's efforts while every decision of the Referee which did not give them an advantage they haoted viciously. Mr. Mainwa,ring was fair to both teams, and erred only on the side of leniency. Yet he got a reception onleaving :the enclosure that would only have been merited had he robbed the home team of the match. He ought to have something to say to the League Committee on the matter. Something more drastic is required thin the publication of warn- ing notices. These a'rea iy stare the • crowd in the face, but they are ignored.

If Warrington 133 I wan last Saturday they might have looked hopefully towards the first four. Even now they are not quite out of the running, fir there is a long sequence of home matches aid prospective victories to come. Wigan ma le no mistake about trouncing Oldham, and once nalre head the table. The League table

The Hull match is always a popular one at Warring- ton, and I anticipate a good erowl at Wit,-lerspool this afternoon. Seeing that Hull only beat the Wire- pullers by 5 points to nil in Yorkshire they should be in for a fairly certain licking to-day. Warrington are fortunate enough to have ail their best players avail- able, including Shugars, whose weight has been required in the pack for some time. Out of their six forwards, Warrington will to-day have four Welsh- men, the only home-grown srcanrnager of the half- dozen being Al! Boardman.
The selected side is : Tilley, fall back; Fish, Dickenson, Taylor and Treharne, three-quarters ; Brooks and Jenkins, half-backs ; O'Neill, Dywoll, Thqmis, Shugars, A.. Boardman ant Balton, forwards.

The third test match was played on Wednesday at Glasgow when the Kangaroos drew with an English side, the score being 17 pointsjeach. England had a big lead until the last quarter, when the Australians put on points in rapid order, and equalised by a goal, which the home players say was a yard out. Wet weather spoiled the attendance, but a fine game wls witnessed, and Dickenson shone with some splendid running and passing. He and Lomas at centre were tw,) of the star players of the side. Brooks was an absentee owing to the death of his brother, the halves being Jolley awl Lilly, b)th of whom payed a clever game.
Runcorn played their poitponed match with B itley this week-, but were unable to check the gallant youths, who are strong canlidates for the first four. Batley won a very hard game by 5 points to 2.

It is fortunate also thit the " A " team has a powerful side available for they play one of their stiffest Combination matches. If they can beat Wigan Highfield to-day at Wigan they should ho practically certain of the Ohampionship, for on matches played they are five points be:ter off than Wigan" A." The latter lost for the second week in succession on Saturday when Oldham beat them by a goal to nil. Wigan Highfield are the only team which has beaten Warrington" A" this season, and that unexpected reverse at Wilderspool in September has to be atoned for to-day.

The "A " team will be : liclntyre, full back; Bradshaw, Jordon, Cartwright, and Hockenhall, threequartera ; Lees and Lloyd, half backs; Naylor, Chesters, Harmer, Bradshaw, P. Boardman, and Hewitt, forwards.

div.head: Re " Invasion Plays."
div.p: Re " Invasion Plays."

the performance of such plays, I presume, the National Service League are trying to spread their views of the necessity of military training for every young man in Britain. The members of the League pooh-pooh the idea of conscription and a "member of N.S.L." writes of "short efficient service " ; but is not this "short efficient service " the thin edge of the wedge? l would advise every young man before he joins the National Service League to get from the Library "Home Life in France" by Miss Betham- Edwards and study the chapter on " Conscripts." To quote from it ;--"4 Then your experience is that conscription does not tend to make young men more patriotic, nor to imbue them with the military spirit?" "Patriotic indeed!" was the reply, " instead conscription turns them into Socialists and Anarchists. Ttit3 German army, as you know, reeks with S )cialism and there is plenty of it.. in our own. As to enforced military service inclining men to soldiering, on the contrary it makes them loathe it. I for one, am all for disarmament and arbitration." That is the speech of one who has suffered the hardships of compulsory military service. Personally, I have seen nothing in France to com- mend the system. In every walk of life man is hampered by it. And what of the womea ? I have soon women scavengers in the towns of France and the " gentler sex" performing such laborious work that an English- man would scorn to pormit in this land. It pained me to see women working 5,3 hard and I asked a French- man why it was allowed? "Conscription is to blame" was the reply. If Englishmen desire not recurring interference with their daily life, if they cherish the women of this land (for after all it is the women who are the greatest sufferers in France) then it tehoves them to resist every attempt to bring about an enforced military service.—Yours truly, A SUPPORTER OF THE INTERNATIONAL BROTHERHOOD ASSOCIATION. The Proposed " Civic League of Help."

Sir,—On behalf of the Provisional Committee appointed to arrange (if found practicable) the forma- don of a Civic League of Help for Warrington, we desire to make a public statement of the progress we have made, and beg that you will grant us space in your valuable paper for that purpose. Investigations and enquiries have been made— influential representatives of the various charitable agencies have been interviewed—and we have now arrived at a stage when we feel justified in calling for public support. With this aim in view we have approached his Worship the Nlayor_and he has kindly expressed his willingness to preside at a public meeting to be held in the Cannon Charuber on Tuesday evening the 9th inst , at 8 o'clock when proposals will be brought forward for the immediate renting of an office in the centre of the town and the advertising for and engage- of a suitable person as paid secretary to undertake the clerical work of the League. With the execution of stationery etc., there will be no other expenditure to provide for, the whole of the operations of the League being carried on by voluntary helpers. At this meeting it is desired that a guarantee of financial support should be obtained which will suffice to cover these expenses,

It is gratifying to be able to state with regard to the raising of funds for the establishment of the League that we have received offers of substantial sums towards the first year's working expenses to be paid over as soon as we can show that we are in a position to begin. We are very anxious, therefore to be able to avail our- selves of these munificent offers and to enable us to do so we seek to influence all who take an interest in social work of any kind to join us in the formation of this desirable League which, we confidently anticipate, will serve a naost useful and beneficent purpose in assisting the existing charitable agencies to discriminate the really deserving, whilst at the same time rendering personal advice and help incases where it is found that effort on the part of the individual seeking help is the chief need. We shall require a fairly large and widely repre- sentative general committee of influential ladies and gentlemen and we trust that all those who were unable from various causes to be present at the previous meet- ing will not fail to come forward and give us their help and counsel on this occasion. We shall also be prepared to receive the names and addresses of those who are able and willing to enrol themselves as helpers and we would especially urge those who have any enthusiasm for work in which a little personal sacrifice is needed to come forward and join in this good work. —We are, sir, yours etc., for the Committee, WM. BRACECAMP, Caairman.

Bank Quay Workingmen's Mission League of Help. Sir,—Since reference was made to the above in our Secretary's recent report many enquiries have been made by persons anxious to know what is being done by the above Leagne. We also note that his Worship the Mayor has called a meeting with a view to inaugurating a civic L3ague of Help for Warrington. We therefore think that a brief account of the league in connection with Bulk Quay Mission may be of interest to the public, and may possibly be helpful to those who are desirous of supporting this wider movement which we hope will shortly be commenced. Oar fink Quay Mission Leigue of Help was formed in November last and has a membership of about 150, each member being a monthly subscriber to the funds. It has not been necessary to appeal to the public for assistance as up to the present subscriptions of mem- bers have met all requirements. We have a working committee of 42 members' representing in sections of 6 the seven main branches of workers in connection with the Mission, i.e. Caurch com- mittee, S3hool committee, Men's cless, Women's class, Young Men's class, Young Women's class and S)ciety class. We have also an executive consisting of 14 members selected in sections of two's from the seven branches of the committee. Tne meet- ings of the executive are held weekly; those of the committee monthly. The work of the league consists in the systematic ir.vestigation of the district selected by the committee, With a view to finding out oases of distress and administering relief as may be thought desirable. Cases due to intemper- ance or disolute habits are not considered. Whenever possible persons in need are advised as to the best methods by which they may help themselves, and where members of a family are out of work the influence of the league is used in assisting them to fled employ- ment. The work is conducted on the broad lines of Caristlen duty and persons assisted without regard to denomination or creed. At the weekly meetings of the executive reports are received in reference to persons in need, and members of the League who have cases to report may attend any weekly meeting of the executive, or any nronthly meeting of the committee for the pur- pose of presenting, such report. The Executive decides what cases to assist and arranges for visitation. There is a clothing department with two secretaries, who arrange for the collection and distribution of clothing, bedding &c. Oar average weekly expenditure has been about £2. The maximum number of families relieved in any one week being 16. We are much indebtel to the Itsv. W. Tiracecamp who in response to an invitation from the Committee gave a valuable address on The Civic Loagne of Help." We sincerely hope that the efforts of his Worship the Mayor, and of others who are so enthusiastic in connec- tion with this most deserving cause, will meet with great success and that the proposed movement will be promptly and generously supported, that in a very short time all the deserving poor in our. town shall be fed and clothed.—Yours truly,
T. DALE.

div.head: Lecture at the Academy.
div.p: Lecture at the Academy.

On Monday eveuing the members of the Warrington Slciety were much interested in a lecture given by Mr. Josiah Longland on "The Less Read Novels of Charles Dickens." The lecturer proved to be a close student and ardent admirer of the voluminous works of the great novelist and depicter of character, and his thoughtful criticism of some of the less known books proved very instructive to the audience. At the close there was an interesttng discussion taken part in by Messrs. Nfadeley, Bennett, Jenkins and Lofthouse, and the lecturer WAS cor&ally thanked for his paper.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
WIDNES SPORTSIcIAN'S ILLNESS.

Widnes sportsmen and those in South-West Lanca- shire who knew him will regret to hear of the sudden illness of Mr. Fred. Wright, the popular treasurer of the Widnes Football Club. lie was at work on Saturday, and went home feeling unwell. Becoming worse, he was taken away to the Widnes Accident Hospital late on Sunday night, and was found to be suffering from appendicitis. An operation was performed. The patient passed a fairly good night.
EXTRAORDINARY MOTOR•CA.R ACCIDENr. CAR FALLS INFO TdE SHIP CANAL.

An extraordinary accident occurred at Runcorn on Monday evenine, when a motor-car fell into the Nfau- chester Ship Canal. The machine brushed aside the protecting clain of the transporter bridge, and as the transporter car was not in dock the motor leapt over the edge and, turning a somersault, dropped on its side into about three feet of water.

There were three occipauts of the motor-car-Ir. Lloyd Jones, tea merchant, Liverpool, who escaped with a shaking ; Mr. Bolton, an elderly gentlsman, of Liverpool, who was severely bruised ; and the chauffeur, Frank Pilling, who fell under the car, and had his head cut and ribs badly bruised.

The chauffeur, seeing the light of the approaching transport, thought he was on the road. The first intima- tion of danger that he had was the chain striking his chin. Needless to say, he had never before been across the river by the bridge, and did not know the way. The oar was a fine new four-seated vehicle, just purchased by Mr. Lloyd Junes,aud the run was intended for his initiation into the art of driving, the challeur having been lent for that purpose by his employer, Mr. Ernest Butterworth, oil merchant, Liverpool and West Kirby. They had been a circular run by way of Ashton- under-Lyne. The injured persons were quickly assisted by Messrs. R. Brisco and Booth, with three other young fellows, and conveyed to a hotel near by, where they were attended by Dr. MacLennAn.
Fortunately tha accident happened when the tide was up otheraiso the car might have fallen on to the bare stoue bed, with disastrous rosult to the o,::cupauts.

div.head: CUT THE TELEGRAPH WIRES.
div.p: CUT THE TELEGRAPH WIRES.
Tngular Charge of Theft at Warrington.

At the Borough Police Ciurt on Monday, Thomas Massy,metal broker,Liverpool-road,and William Clarke, au employee of the first prisoner, were charged with stealing and receiving 281bs of copper wire, value 225., the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company. The Chief Constable stated that early on the morning of Wednesday last, the wire was cut from the telegraph poles, between Rink Cinay Station and the Walton Arches, thus interrupting the connection between London and Liverpool. The police were infor:ned, and detective Reddington made inquiries. Ile went to various metal brokers in the town, including a Mr. Howard, giving descriptions of the stolen wire. It was subsequently found that a quantity of copper wire had been sold to Mr. Howard by the prisoner Massey. Detective Reddington repeatedly called at Massey's shop but he denied all knowledge of the thefts. Subse- quently from information received by the police. Massey and Clarl/4e were taken into custody and brought to the Police Station. It was then found that Clarke himself ha,i delivered the wire at the premises of Mr. Howard. When charged at the Police Station, Massey said : "I got it but I don't know where I got it from. I plead guilty." The chief constable asked for a remand of 8 days in order that inquiries might be instructed regarding the stolen property. Mr. T. S. Steel, who appeared for both prisoners, applied for bail. He hoped that when the case came up for hearing he would be able to pat a different com- plexion upon it. The prisoner Massy had an extensive business to carry on, and he could not possibly carry it on while in prison. Heasked the magistrates to grant bail to the two prisoners. The Chief Constable opposed the granting of hail on the ground that the prisoners had not in any way helped the police while instituting inquiries regarding the theft of the wire.
-. • The bench dtscussod the matter in private and on their return the Chairman (the Mayor) stated that tha application for bail was refused.

Annie Ryder' aged eleven years, of Caancery-lans, Parr, died in the 6t. Helens Hospital, early on lionday morning from burns. The girl was engaged, along with her mother, on 6unday morning, by the fireside, when her clothing took fire, and though the mother made every effort to stay the progress of the flames, the Injuries were such that death resulted. LABOUR MEETING AT ST. HELENS.

Ifr. T. Glover, on Monday night attended the annual reunion of the St. Helens Labour party, which was held at the Town Hall. Tuere was a goon attend- ance. Mr. A. Rudd presided, and Said the Labour party was the only one that was lighting the people's cause, and they would win in the end. Tne people mast rule, and even iu St. Helens, where they had great powera arrayed against them, the time would come when the people would have their way. Mr. Glover said he believed most firmly that the Labour party had come to stay. Nine yeari ago their party gathered together. in connection with the Trades Union CJagress, and they made up their minds that the time had acme for the. working classes of the country to have their position improved, sad that itvres time that more men were sent from their own ranks to Parliaaient for the purpose of s4curing attention to their vrarn..s and of passing laws which would benefit the workers. From that time the party had increased from a reprecen;ation Of 300,uthl people to close on 2,0J0,01/0, which was ample proof of the great progress the party was making. At Newton Patty Sessions lust Thursday, Jamcs Ratcliffe and Edward Winstauley were charged with a game trespass on January 9th at Golborne.—Mr. Arthur .Browne, prosecuting for Lord Newton, suid it was en impudent case. The men supposed that if they remained on the highway and their dog went on the the land and caught a hare, which they killed, they could not Le punished because they had not left the high road. That was what happened, and Winstanley put the hare into a bag and took it away.— John Hart, of Swell Brow, IVigan, said be was in a little hothouse by the side of the road, and hearing something went out and saw a dog with a hare. Ratcliffe took it and gave it to William Wiustanley, who killed it and put it inn bag, saying it was his and he was going to have it.—Mr. White said there was not much dispute ea to the facts. But there is no reason why old folks should endure these painful chest-troubles ; for in the novel Peps tablets a wonderful breathe-able medicine has been concentrated which is now recognised as the ideal remedy for old-age coughs, because the medicine is breathed direct through the throat and bronchial tubes to the seat of the trouble. One or two Peps at night ensure healthy and unbroken sleep, while one or two on rising in the morning clear the breathing tubes of the accumulated phelgra and •impurities. of the night and thus promote comfort and ease during the day time. div.head: OUR LOCAL CIIIEGFIES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CIIIEGFIES.
Rev. R. E. Letheren and the Opium Trade.

The Bev. 11. E. I.:ltheren in the course of his sermon at the Baptist Church,Golborne-street,on Sunday morn- ing, referred to the International C•mmission for the investigation of the opium trade and the opium habit in Chinn, which was to open its sittings at Shanghai on the following day. He referred to the King's Spe, 31k on the propogation of Parliament, in which it was stated that the Commission would meet with a view of assisting China in her purpose of eradicating the opium trade in the Chinese Empire. Teat Conference would. have grave issues, and it was to urge Christian people to pray that God would so direct the deliberatiors of the Commissioners that they might take action for the abolition of the traffic that he brought the matter before them. The trade had been !declared by the House of Commons to be morally Indefensible, and yet righteousness was spurned for the sake of revenue. Lie then referred to the friendly over- tures of the United States, whose hands were clean of this business, as the outcome of which this Inter- national Commission had been arranged. It was an opportuaity for the nation to return to the way of righteousness, and shake itself free of the shackles of a stupendous sin. It was righteousness that exalted a. nation. To continue in ways they confessed to be morally indefensible was as mad as it was bad, and must end in disaster. It might be that the return to righteousness would entail some present sacrifice. Il was convinced that even on the level of prosperity Great Britain bad lost Jar more through this trade than the Indian revenues had gained. It was for Christiaft people who loved their land and held its honour dear to! pray God so to guide this crisis in affairs that Great. Britain might no longer contribute to the worlds wretchedness by this wrong-doing to its own moral weakening,

ening of New Premises Celebratd.

A tea, concert and dance were therefore held in the Parr Hall -on Tht.rsday evening and proved highly successful and enjoyable. About 500 sat down to an excellent tea. the -catering being in the hands of Atkinson's Cafe's, Ltd. At the concert Mr. 13. The Society began in a small way, but now they bed a turnover of nearly £4,000 per week. Now that they were able to conduct their business under snore favourable conditions, with the splendid new premises and the increased ntynber of branches, they hoped that with the loyal support of the members they would dnuble that turnover before runny years had passed. div.head: COMPULSORY MILITARY TRAINING.
div.p: COMPULSORY MILITARY TRAINING.
ARTICLE hr.— CoscLustox.
The Advantages.
AN ALLEGORY.

. Once upon a time there was a public school, which was fast losing its old fame. The boys slouched in the streets ; examination results were poor ; football matches were invaribly lost, since some boys always forgot to attend. The bond of discipline had been slackened. Then came a new headmaster, who after consultation with the parents, introduced compulsory games. Did the boys get less keen on games because they were compelled to turn up on the football field regularly? Not at all. The result was an increase of keenness all round. All felt that they were doing their share for the school. The bort became united in a real esprit•de corps. Fresh air and regular exercise enabled them to work at books with greater mental 'rigour and freshness. The first eleven volun- tarily got up early in the morning and indulged in training runs. In a word the school prospered because all its members did their duty. This is a true story.

div.head: OUR MORAL-D'ANGER.
div.p: OUR MORAL-D'ANGER.

But it is also symbolical of the state of England to-day. In both municipal life and national life, too heavy a burden is being put on the willing horse. As an acute Japanese critic said, "You English are always howling,abut your rights; you say nothing of your duties: If any reader does not believe this condemnation, let him ask for the opinion of the nearest minister of religion, or doctor ; ask any friend who comes in close contact with his fellowmen. Study Mr. Charles Booth's statistics as to the infinitesmal numbers in London, who ever enter a place of worship. Let him ask him- self whether the watchword of vast numbers of the leisured classes rnly not be summed up in the simple formula " Why worry ? " whether there are not thousands and thousands of people lower down in the strata of society who consider that their one duty in life i to save money and to save their souls, and never to give a thought to the saving of their country; whether there are not still more on the bedrock of society who, very largely as a result of the neglect of those who should have been their leaders, are nom coming to think that their main duty in life is to get rich quick by the attractive method of legislative grab. From all sides evidences of moral dangers sweep in upon us. In both the criminal classes and the unemployable leisured classes on will find the same characteristics • the same insuperable aversion to steady work, the same self-indulgence, the same eager devotion to the interests of the moment. THE PHYSICAL DANGER.

Dr. A. B. Meyer, the Director of the Zological Museum at Dresden, described in an official report a visit to the Peel Park Museum, at Salford, where be saw a kind of people, "who happily are not known in German musemns,because in our larger German towns we have not so degenerate a population." The need to secure that every youth in Germany shall be physically fit for military training has kept the attention of the nation on the need to counteract the bad influence of town life. One of the greatest instruments for this is the use of military drill and gymnastics into all schools. The National Service League lays the greatest possible emphasis on the immediate necessity of introducing compulsory military drill in all schools and the encouragement of cadet corps and boys' brigades. With that aim the Lads' Drill Association is incorporated with the National Service League. But the physical dangers are not confined to the youth of the nation. I read in the annual report (Cd 4401) of the Registrar General of Births, Deaths and Marriages in 1907, just pub- li.hed, that the marriage rate in 1907, when compared with that of 1870-80, shows a fall of 10.4 per cont., and that the crude birth-rate of 20 3 per 1,000 of the total population is the lowest on record. I read lin the last Army Medical Department Report that 95 Iper cent of the recruits are out of etnployment at the time of enlistment and in poor condition. I read that 281 is the ratio per 1,000 of men rejected on inspec- tion. In 1815 our s.andard height Wes sft. Gins., and the population under that was 105 per 1,090. In 1887 the proportion under sft. Gins. was 528, and in 1901 it was 595 per 1,030. But even the French under universal military training are gradually improving in stature, so are the Italians and the Austrians. To what abyss of physical degeneration is town-life without counteracting conditions going to lead us? The future is a serious question to face to the statistics quoted above. It does not much matter whether we were in past ages elevated from superior apes, or descended from archangels, but it does matter that many a boy in our board schools is as badly developed:aq the ma:um-grinder's monkey.

div.head: ME REMEDY MORALLY.
div.p: ME REMEDY MORALLY.

It is high time for the man in the street to arouse the man in the Cabinet to realise the invasion of apathy which is creeping over us all. There is much to he said for ,those who assert that they would welcome a millitary invasion if it would stop the ever- increasing tnoral and physical invasion. But many experts believe that we may stop both invasions by the introduction of compulsory military training. The national complaint is very like the school complaint. In both nation and school the enforcement of a common duty reveals to all the need of individual training arid the value of individual effort. Each member of a football team or a military company knows that the perfection of the whole depends on himself. He knows that bi failure brings discreiit on the whole. So both the boy and tho citizen soldier learn the true ideals of social unity and social relationship, giving the schoolboy a belief in the school traditions, and the citizen soldier a genuine faith in himself and his conntrv. VOLUNTARY CO \ (.7LSI DN.

That is the true answer to those who say com- pulsory training will stop voluntary recruiting for our regular army. Those who say so, either use the "word well-smoothen" or have never troubled to staly the militsry systems of other European Country. Take Ssitzerland as an example. where the proposals of the National Service Leigue,(i e. drill in all schools and training for the youth), are aetudly in practice. Has that killed the voluntary spirit of which wog English are supposed to hold the monop Ay ? No! Although Switzerland is only half the size of Ireland, it has over 200,000 members of voluntary rifle clubs. Great Britain has under 80,000 members. In Switzerland there are HI hospital orations with 7,233 members and a Red Cross Association with 18,071 members, Pontoon sections, Officers & N.C.O.'s Tactical S ,cieties, Balloon Sections, and a Motor Corps, and all this work is voluntary. There are 41,030 officers, yet all the necessary time and work given to rise from a private is voluntary. ( Territorial officers may be interested to learn that it is necessary to put in 203 (lays' trainine in Switzerland, before becomine a Lieutenant.) Where is our molopely of the voluntary spirit ? Far better is the spirit of praetical patriotism embodied in the law of universal service.

IVESLEYANS AND THE LORDS.

div.head: "All but a Handful" in Favour of the Licensing Bill.
div.p: "All but a Handful" in Favour of the Licensing Bill.

There has been quite a stir caused among Wesleyan% recently by the acute controversy which has arisen out of the declaration by the President of the Conference lhe Rev. J. Scott Lidgett, who at. the recent anniver- sary of the Manchester Central Mission said he had written to Lord Lansdowne, telling him that if the Lords rejected the Licensing Bill they would do an act which " will never either be forgotten or forgiven by the Wesleyan Methodist Church." For this declaration the President has been criticised by the " Methodist Recorder " for attempting to embroil the Wesleyan Church in a political controversy The" Methodist Recorder "has taken up the position that the Wesleyan Church ought to stand aside from politics. Its the" Methodist. Times," of which he is the editor, the Rev. J. Scott Lidget has replied with vigour contending that on an issue which involves the moral and social well-being of thetation,the Wesleyan Church cannot stand aside.

Speaking recently at Newport, Isle of Wight. the President said : " Some have talked of my identifying Methodism with politics. Ido not identify Methodism with a political party. I identify it with the business of Jesus Christ. He who thinks only of the peace of Methodism will lose peace, but he who thinks of the glory of Christ will gain it and the peace of Methodism as well. Spiritual progress and intellectual progress must be aided by an enlightened and progressive administration. Let it be known that Methodism stands for spiritual work, for progress, and for the interests of humanity. We want so to act that the House of Lords will know there are earnest, ardent, inspired men and women about, and not only brewers and their friends. The Rev. J. E. Rattenhury, the well-known Wesleyan missior er,who spoke the other evening at a public meet- ing to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the founding of the Bridgwater Hallalulme,told a representative of" The Dail3 News "that the idea that Wesleyans are divided on this question is unfounded. " Nine hundred and ninety-nine Wesleyans out of a thousand," said Mr. Rattenbury, "know exactly where they stand, and thst is for temperance and licensing reform without qualifica- tion. A few, a very few, wealthy Conservatives sup- port the view that on this question the church should be passive, but they are not one-tenth per cent."

LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
Another Discussion on Tariff Reform.

Alderman Bennett's Bill for the Federation of the Empire has certainly been productive of a most interesting debate and the speeches at Tuesday evening's meeting of the Parliamentuy Thbating Society were of a high order which did the members credit. There was again a large attendance and the discussion was followed with keen enthusiasm.

Mr. W. MAsoN (1., Newcastle-under-Lyne) who re-opened the debate, had a preliminary 'tilt at" the fatuity and uselessness of party government." He supported the Bill in its entirety', although he was sorry the clause dealing with the *fiscal policy had been included, because it might mean the losing of the measure. If they took out the fiscal paragraph the whole Bill could be accepted by the Opposition as their party politics. (Opposition cries of" No.") He was not afraid of Tariff Reform, though he was a very tardy Tariff Reformer, because he was a believer in universal Free Trade which we had not now and which it was quite possible we never should have. Because he was a believer in Free Trade, however, he was not compelled to swallow the fly-blown imitation which n embers of the Liberal party for generations had worshipped as a fetish. Ever since he remembered, the Liberal party had been boiling over with anger against the House of Lords, but it still flourished like a green kay tree. (Laughter.)'rho A!ember for Dundee put his thumb into the measure, pulled out a plum and when he found it bore the letters "T.R." he began to belabour it with leather and tomatoes. (Laughter.) The Bill embodied reform of the House of Lords and the House of Commons and would draw closer the bond of union between the colonies and the Mother Country.He could draw quite different conclusions from the loss of the American colonies from those drawn by the Deputy- Leader of the Opposition (Mr. W. Furness). Those colonies were lost because this country did not take them into their confidence, and did not make them partners in the firm, with a full share of the dividend accruing from the Empire. Mr. J. Et.wEr.r„ JUN. (L., Wednesbury) asked what was to be the basis of federation. Were the small handful of white men in some of the colonies going to elect the members of the Imperial Parliament, or were all the inhabitants to have the same voice in the Government? Were the colonies to be permitted to retain their present high tariffs against the mother country. Of what value was a preference if the first wall over which we had to leap was unclimbable ? They complained of foreign countries erecting their tariff walls, and yet, the self-governing colonies erected barriers that were higher. At present IVO gave the Colonies free and open ports and paid for their 'defence but they did not reciprocate. He contended that the C ilonies were not in favour of Free Trade with the E npire and he strongly objected to any tariffs being placed upon the necessaries of life, be,canse those least able to pay wauld have to bear the burden. Mr. R. DONE (C. Newport) gave an unualified support to the Bill because it was a step in the right direction. It was only natural that the Opposition should oppose the Bill because they were carrying on the policy of Cobden and Bright who were opposed to the C lonies betng attached to the British E.npire. It was a fallacy to say it was always the best to buy in the cheapest market, regardless of the cost of production or the wages paid. Mr. Parker spoke about the present "level terms "which meant that we purchased in the cheapest market, whether the goods came from sweated BAgiura or anywhere else. Mr. PARKER.: I was speaking of the matter from an economic point of view. If wo were discussing the question of sweating I should probably boat one with our friend.

Mr. DJNE said Free Traders put the consumer's interests before the producer's, but to the workingman that was like p:ittino,* the cut before the horse. At present we were free to buy but not free to sell, so we had not Rot Free Trade.

Mr. Monts (N., Ssotland Division of Liverpool) opposed the Bill because of its many unconstitutional elements. If the measure became law, it was not bind- ing on the Government to call an Imperial Conference. Federation was an alluring picture and an ideal worthy of serious °Rests, but he believed it could be attained by simpler means and with greater freedom than by a system of Protection. He further opposed the Bill because of the clause relating to Protection. He claimed that a tariff raised against materials or food stuffs would set back the development of our industries and would be against the best interests of the people of these islands. With regard to the iron and steel trade, thousands of tons of ore were imported annually to keep, our blast furnaces in operation, because our own ores were not sullicient or were not of the right quality. Alderman Bennett said he would not tax raw materials, but there were many other things revired to be imported, in addition to ore, for the manufacture of iron and steel. Mr. Rigby (rioted a long list and said the cost of almost the whole of those' things %could be a ivanced by exactly the amount of the tariff raised against them. (Applause.) Wao imagined for a moment that the Calonial exporter would reduce his price a single bawbee lower than the cost of manu- facture plus a profit and plus another profit which was equal to the amount of the tariff raised • against the goods of his foreign competitor? Men he got used to that amount of profit, he would be agitating for more and more tariff. Protection absolutely failed to keep out manufactured articles from Germany and the United S ales of America. We beat the whole world at shipping but the United States had Protection and their shipping had dwindled. Germany was now admitting free the imports of all materials used in the construction and equipment of ships. It, was un ler the fostering wing of Protection that the great trusts were nurtured. Mr. J. Ilow'Es, jolts., (L., Lancaster) said the C donial Secretary should have termed his Bill the "Set the Empire to Rights Bill." (Laughter.) The proceeds of the tariff were to be administered for imperial defence. What a wonderful proposition! A shilling in the £ and the Empire was sa.e. (Laughter.) Had it not occurred to the Colonial Sacretary that the taxation of ground rents and royalties would bring in more revenue with the additional advantage that it would be paid by the rich instead of by the very poor? (Applause.) HA he forgotten that Mr. Chamberlain declared: "If you give a preference to the C slonies, you must tax the people's food"? Hid tariff- reformers turned their backs on Mr. Chamberlain, after all he had done for them? (Ministerial Criesa of " N).") Then they must tax the people's food. (Oeposition Casters.) All the existing tariff) had been imposed by the party to which the C Sacretary belonged. Toe Liberal party had been abolishing and reducing these national burdens with the result that the country had increased in prosperity and happiness. He (Mr. Howes) was a tariff reformer, because he would reform all tariffs out of existence. All our imports came here in ships and were paid for by exports which went out in ships. Stop the goods from coming in and we would not require ships to bring them. If they did not corns in, we would not have to pay for them; therefore we would not need to manufacture the goods that went out as exports in payment for the imports. Tim first result would be to strike a blow at shipping and, incidentally, at the coal industry. Federation forsooth! Tee scheme the C olonial S)cretary proposed to federate the Empire did not even federate the great Tory party. (levighter.) Narnbers of their members were in open revolt against the tariff proposals and tbe great con- stitetional party had had. to bring into existence a band of conspirators whoa e names were not revealed but who were known as Clnfederates, for the purpose cif driving out of the party all who would not subscribe to the vague and undefined programme of the tariff reformers. The great constitutional party had turned moonlighters. (I, anglater.) -.What a sight for the gods ! (Laughter.) Tariff reform, he contendel in conclusion, stood for the tyranny of the .few against the liberty of the many. (Opposition cheers.) The Parmlil MrNETEa (Mr. W. H. Stansfleld), said ho found from the " Examiner " rep3rt that two Liberal leaders did not agree, for whereas the member for Bristol (Mr. W. Farness) said the Bill was too broad and generous to be eCniservativemoasurs, the member for Dundee (Mr. C E.Parker)declared it to be altogether ' bad. The Bill prop3sed to federate the Empire and it would not only retaie all the sentiment spoken of by the Opposition but it would also got some material advantage. The whole Bill breathed a business spirit and tackled questions which the Opposition dare not tackle. It would pet the House of Lord on a democratic basis. Federation, he contended, had made G2rmany the world power it now was. Taking it for granted that the Colonies were the greatest sinners in the matter of tariffs, representation in the Imperial Parliament and intercourse with ourselves would pos- sibly have the effect of modifying the tariffs and would eventually bring about red Free Trade within the Empire. The member for Dandee (Mr. Parker) made a point of the fact that Bradford traders imported their wool from the Colonies and would therefore not have to bear their share of the tariff. It must not be over- looked, however, that the wool when introduced into this country provided work and wages for our people. We could do very well without the tomatoes that Mr. Parker spoke abont,but we could not do without wool and therefore if Bradford did escape the tariff we would be netting the advantage all through. Tu conclusion the Prime Minister disclaimed any intention on the part of the G overnment of forcing the scheme on the Calonies. It was a matter for mutual agreement. Mr. RATIIRONE (L., Exeter) opposed the Bill because the tariff reform clause was economically unsound as well as unjust and would lead to endless dissatisfaction and ultimately to the disruption instead of the Federation of the Empire. The more one examined the proposition the more one became convinced that it was based on a very superficial grasp of the Situation. Mr. J.MeDEßasto (Paisley) moved the adjournment of the debate, and this was agreed to.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
" Peter's Mothr."

"Peter's Mother,": one of the most pleasing comedies ever seen here, is presented at the Royal Court Theatre this week by Miss Emma and Mr. Percy Hutchison's company. Comedy though it is, and while there is no lack of genuine humour, a strong vein of pathos gives the play an aided power. Its very simplicity constitutes a charm and the audience cannot but follow with keenest interest the fortunes of the woman struggling 'twixt love and duty, yet never failing in devotion to her soldier son even when —unconsciously it is true —he behaves most selfishly towards her. The tone of the play is distinctly high throughout; the story is cleverly woven, and the character studies a-e drawa w"th wonder- ful skill. " Peter's Mother" is one of the most lovable of stage personages, and Miss Violet Ley gives a maguiticent interpretation of the part. Her winsomeness of manner, her alternating moods of joyousness arid despair, the soulfulness waich she infuses into her acting all conspire to win. the hearts of the audience, and prove her to be a true attiste. Mr. Drew Mackintosh is almost equally convincing as John Crewys, Q.C.J., —a part to which he is eminently suited. One of the finest passages in the play is that in which he reasons with Peter and vividly paints the injustice and harshness of a course of action which wiuld consign a woman, filled with life and spirits, to a monotonous and colourless existence at the age of thirty-eight. Mr. Vivian Gilbert achieves a brilliant success as the brave and impetuous yet priggish "Peter" in fact one could hardly imagine a finer impersonation. Mr. Townsend Whiffing makes the most of the role of Sir Timothy Crewys, Bart., which affords him but few opportunities, his portrayal of the stern knight who treats his wife as a child, being thoroughly realistic. Mr. Walter Russell is admirable as tin kind-hearted Canon Burch, who is fated to mention subjects which t) Sir Timothy are as the red rag to the bull.. Miss Hilda Sims is a gay and impetuous Sarah and dr. Edward Jephson displays talent of a high order as Dr. Blundell. Mach of the humour of the piece is provided by Miss Mary Griffiths and Miss Josephine Ray, who take the parts of the virtuous and interfering sisters, Lady Belstone and Miss G. Crewys, to the life. The play is well mounted, the last scene which depicts the garden at Barra° nnbe Manse being exceptionally beautiful. As a curtaia riser " Turtle Divas," a farce in one act, is much above the average.

I aivise them invariably to go to their chemist, and get one half-ounce of Marrnola (be careful to get a sealed packa3e) one ounce of fluid extract of Glycyrrhiz.n,B.P., one ounce of pure Glycerine and Peppermint Water to mike six ounces in all. These ingredients can be mixed together at home or by your chemist. Take two teaspoonfuls after meals and at bedtime. "All these are simple, wholesome remedies that cannot do harm to anyone. They greatly improve the health. while the tapil decrease of fat is truly astonish- ing. I htve known a woman •to lose over thirty pounds between visits to me. NER
OUSNESS IN THE FIELD.
KET

It requires a good deal of nerve to enter the cricket field, conscious of thousands of carping critics feasting their eyes upon you; and at the wicket one must have still greater confidence if one wants to make even a passable display. Most of our leading cricketers have, at one time or another, made egregious asses of themselves, through sheer nervousness.

Witness the .occasion, for instance, at Lord's some years ago, when a University batsman, being overcome with fear, made a rush for the pavilion when called upon by his partner for a run. Incidents of this kind are not uncommon. in county cricket matches.

As one of the crowd, it is very easy to comment on a man's play. The unobserved and irresponsible onlooker has no idea of the agonies endured by a young batsman who, realising the greatness of the occasion, loses his held altogether and throws away his opportunities.

- When Dr. Grace was a young man, he created something of a sensation at the Oval by hitting a ball :ipparently out of sight, i.nd running till he and his partner almost sank to the ground exhausted. What had happened was this: the Doctor played but missed a slow ball, which actually entered las breast picket unnoticed, his nervousness rendering him unconscious of the sudden

Seeing the Doctor's magnificent stroke, but ignorant of the ball's whereabouts, Gr-ce's partner called for a run, the fielders. marvelling meanwhile at the mysterious disappearance of the ball. The two batsmen, however, continued to run, till the wonderful stipposed hit was worth a dozen runs. At last Dr. Grace, while trying to reeover his breath, put his hand to his heart, and immediately after produced the long- lost ball to the indescribable astonishment of everybody present._

Some curious cricket is frequently the out- come of nervousness. There arc many cases on record where the " first man in" has made a duck's egg in the first innings, but has kept a cool head and scored a "century" in the second. Nervous bowlers are an extreme danger, as many readers are doubtless aware.

north country cricket team was 'once disgraced by their bowler sending five \vides in succession. Another bowler, suffering from an attack of nervousness, actually threw the ball at the wicket and nearly brained the batsman. Fielders, again, often make themselves the butt of unseemly jokes. On the 13righ ton cricket ground a few years ago one of the Sussex men, while , guarding the boundary, mistook a round stone for the ball, and threw it up to the wicket. The blunder was not discovered till the crowd groaned at seeing the real ball fly to the boundary. _

One of the most extraordinary results of nervousness in the cricket field was witnessed in Calcutta sonic little time ago. A match was fixed between an English team and an eleven consist•ng of harmless lunatics from an asylum in the neighbourhood. The English team won the toss and .went in first. It was not long before a ball found its way to the lunatic cricketer placed in the long field. This poor fellow evidently became unnerved, seized the ball, and ran as fast as his legs could carry him away from the ground. The other lunatic fielders, seeing their com- rade neglecting his duty, made a. dash also, knd the whole ten lunatics were seen running after the fugitive across the surrounding fields. A chase ensued, the like of which had never been seen before, and the English captain thought well to de lac the innings closed after the extraordinary cAlapse of the other side.
THE BICYCLE THIEF AGAIN.
The bicycle thief is inventive this year.

A young man was practising chiles in front of his house, when two fellows stopped on the pavement to admire him. One of them asked how much the wheel weighed, and the young man said it weighed 221 b. The smaller of the two •said that was too light, and that he believed in wheels weighing at least 301 b. Also he mentioned that he once came in first in a ten-mile race and rode a wheel weighing 381 b. At this the larger of the strangers laughed derisively, and said : "What do you know about wheels?" "Why, I've ridden more wheels than you ever saw," replied the other. "I don't believe you can ride at all." " l'll bet you a sovereign I can. Let me show him on your wheel. 1 won't hurt it." He could ride all right. He wobbled slowly on the wheel for a short distance, and then he swished around the corner and was away like the wind. _

"You'd better run after that fellow," said the big stranger; "I don't know him." The owner of the wheel set off, but the short stranger must have been a mile away by that time. Then when the owner came back the big stranger also had gone.
"Do you think Skinner can make a living out there ? " _ .
"Make a living Why, he'd make a living on a rock in the middle of the ocean—if there was another man on the rock."

Attorney (for the defence): "Now, what time was it when you were attacked?" . Complainant: "I don't know; ask your client —he took my watch."

"Women are traditionally supposed to be allowed to wear what they will, and accord- ingly they sometimes wear the most extra- ordinary things. In my business," said a prominent West End jeweller to a contributor, "you see how eccentric some women can be. The usual things we sell in the way of brooches, bracelets, etc., are quite too conventional, and if an article isn't odd, unfamiliar, or oulre, then there is no sale for it. " One of the oddest bracelets I have ever made was that for an American lady, whose husband had succumbed to the bite of a rattlesnake. The venomous reptile was captured and killed. The lady decided to have the snake's skin made into bracelets, with a silver setting. These I .prepared, and now she- may be occasionally seen in society with the • identical bracelets on her arm. The eyes of the rattlesnake are diamonds, each of which is worth £5OO, while the tail is similariy decorated with the precious Stone. " Beetles were, and still are, among some ladies' fityourite articles of decoration. One lady—a peeress I should say, and an enthusiastic entomologist—was out on an insect-catching expedition when she suddenly saw a beautiful beetle rarely, if ever, found in the south country wood she was exploring. She im- mediately caught the insect, and was so taken with it, that she sent it to me to be made into a brooch. The dead' insect was kept for a few days undergoing some embalming process, and then I made it into one of the most • weird, yet beautiful, brooches I have seen. The polished back of the beetle shone like ebony, and the insect's eyes being replaced by diamonds, the 'effect was most brilliant. Time total cost of the beetle was 00. " It is by no means unusual for a lady to bring me her first baby's first tooth to be made into a brooch. An American lady, recently in London, had a tooth made up in this fashion, set hi a perfect nest of diamonds. The cost of that little work of art was £250. "An eye made into a brooch doesn't sound very pleasant, but is what a lady in London wears Iler husband had his face severely injured whilst shooting, the actident necessi- tating the removal of an eye. His wife now wears the eye!" the jeweller laconically con- cluded, with a smile.
A LESSON TO BRIC-A-BRAC BUYERS.
A collector of bric-a-brac lately paid dearly for his hobby. He took a fancy to an antique: vase in a shop. •

The dealer said he would let him have it for but added that, had he the vase tormatch, the pair would be cheap at L'6(:). The collector however declined to buy the odd one. Some clays later he happened to be walking in another part of London and saw in a curiosity Shop a vase, the fellow, apparently, of the one he had lately declined to buy. After a feverish bargain the dealer parted with this vase for £lO. Elated with joy, the purchaser drove to the other shop to secure the first vase, only to learn that it had been sold for Eti to a dealer a few days previously. It was, in fact, the very article he had just bought.
ANOTHER BAD CASE.

We remember the stories of the absent- minded man Who put his umbrella to bed and stood behind the door all night, and of another man who couldn't find his pipe when he had it between his teeth. Here is still another story to add to the list.

A prominent professor who resides ia Birmingham, was hurrying, ill company with a friend, to catch a train, when he stopped suddenly, and exclaimed : "There, I've come away from the hotel and left my watch under the pillow." "Let's go back and get it," said It's friend. "Hold on," said the professor, "I don't believe we shall have time," and he drew the lost watch from his pocket, looked carefully at the face of it, counted the minutes, and added, "No, we sha'n't have time." Then he pressed on towards the station, saying, "Oh well, I think I can get along for one day without a watch."
_+- SMART !

A comedian in a Paris theatre recently made a great hit out of a painful incident. While' indulging in a bit of horse-play on the stage he struck his head violently, entirely by accident, against one of the pillars of the scene upon the stage. On hearing the thud everybody uttered a cry. "No great harm done," said the comedian. "Just hand me a napkin, a glass of water, and a salt-cellar."
These were brought, and he sat down, folded the napkin in the form of a bandage, dipped it in the glass, and emptied the salt-cellar on the wet part.
ILivini thus prepared a compress according to prescription, and when everyone expected he would apply it to his forehead, he gravely rose and tied it round the pillar.

div.head: PHOTOGRAPHIC NOTES.
div.p: PHOTOGRAPHIC NOTES.
By Veronica.
LANTERN SLIDES.

I suppose the majority of lantern slides that are made by amateurs are produced by contact p.rinting, and in these cases it is chiefly by those who work quarter. plate size. For those working larger sizes, it means reduction in the camera, a method many fight shy of, but this should not be the case, as with a little ingenuity an arrangement can easily be made for pro- ducing these easily. I went into a friend's house a short while ago, and found the following contrivance that he had rigged up for this work. Ile got one of the ordinary wooden chocolate boxes that are common in most confectioners' shops, of the size about 9 by 7 by 3. He had taken off the lid, and cut out a space in the bottom of the box the size of his negative, which was whole plate. Across the corners of the openings he had put on little strips of wood to make a rebate to hold the negative, and on the other side little brass catches were screwed on to fix the negative in with. This box frame be then screwed on to one end of a board about six feet in length. He then fitted it up against the window frame at an angle of about 45 degrees, so as to point towards the -sky. The other end of the board was fixed to an upright, which was made secure in the floor. He put his negative in the improvised frame, and to equalise the amount of light passing through the negative, this was also covered by a piece of transparent paper. The camera was adjusted to the right distance from the negative and then clamped by moans of an ordinary thumb screw. When once correct focus had been obtained, he was able to proceed with his lantern slide making from various negatives without any alteration of focus. Intervening space between the negative and the•camera was covered over with a cloth, £0 that no light entered the lens except that coming through the negative. Of coarse his camera, which was a half-plate one, had to be fitted with a carrier inside his dark slides, so as to take the lantern size (3i x 31), and also the same space was mailed on his focussing screen.

div.head: NEW INTENSIFIER.
div.p: A NEW INTENSIFIER.

In nearly all intensification formulae, mercury is recommended for use, but it has one great drawback that is its being so highly poisonous. There is very often a difficulty to obtain it from a chemist unless they know you very well, and for what purpose you require it, and many photographic dealers are not chemists, and they are consequently prohibited under the Poisons Act from selling this. To meet this difficulty a now intensifier has been put upin the market, called " Agfa " Copper Intensifier. As this preparation is non-poisonous, it is a much safer chemical to have in a house. The same firm have also introduced a very handy little flash lamp, which I saw in operation a day or so ago. it is in the form of a little metal folding tray, with a handle to hold the instrument when firing. An ordinary safety match is fixed in the bottom of the tray, and'a little magnesium powder is poured in as well. There is a mechan- ism, consisting of a spring which is released by one'sfinger, which ignites the match and also the powder. It is a most ingenious little :arrangement, and is well worth a trial for any of those interested in flashlight work, as the cost is only trifling.

div.head: PHOTOGRAPHY IN ADVERTISING.
div.p: PHOTOGRAPHY IN ADVERTISING.

The utilisation of photogrophs for advertising pur- poses is not reads use of in this country anything like to the same extent as it is in America, but I notice it is very much on the increase here. One of the latest moves in this direction is a sports and pastimes calendar, that has been issued by Ilford, Ltd., in the form of a little booklet, containing many attractive photographic illustrations.

div.head: EXHIBITION AWARDS.
div.p: EXHIBITION AWARDS.

Many of the photographic societies are deviating from the old custom of giving medals as awards, and supplementing these by plaques, and, in some cases, silvar and bronze bowls, jugs, etc., of artistic design. A very pleasing innovation has been made by the Nottingham Photographic Society in this direction, for their coming exhibition the awards take the form of artistic statuettes.

div.head: TRIPOD ATTACHMENT.
div.p: A TRIPOD ATTACHMENT.

When using a tripoe stand for portraiture in a room, it is often difficult in manipulation. A useful method of getting over this trouble, and having something of the advantage of a studio stand, is to make a little triangle of stripe of wooden battens, about 2ft. 6in. long, on the bottom of which throe castors are fixed. Holes have to be cut out for the tripod feet to go into. By the use of this you can easily push your camera a little nearer to or farther away from your sitter, with- out having to make any alteration as to the height of the camera.

' Missing Caretaker Found Drowned. • The body of John Burgess, aged GE years, of 82, Dalton-bank, caretaker of Fairfield Sch iols, who had been missing since December 23rd, was recovered from the Bridgewater Canal at Latchford on Tuesday morning.—The inquest was held at the Police Station in the afternoon when William Grieve Burgess, s n of the deceased said his father left the house early on on December 23rd, apparently to go to his work. Later he NV.IS seen in Church-street about 6.30 by a Mr. Kenwright. Kenwight said to him, "You are out early. John, this morning" His father answered " Yes; I have not been so well, and I am just going for a walk and a bit of exercise. Deceased had an accident a short time before he left home, and be had always got up with a headache ever since. Witness had no reason to suspect that he would have taken away his life. The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned."
