"THE DRIEST ELECTION." Henry Marshall, employed at the Longford gas works, said he remembered seeing Mr. Peacock in West-street about mid-day on November 12th. Ho said he wanted to see him and witness told him he had not much time. , On the following night between six and seven o'clock Mr. Peacock came and wanted him to sign a paper. He did not show him the paper because witness told him not to bother. Mr. Peacock said it contained a state- ment of bribery against Mr. Rushworth to the effect that Mr. Rushworth had paid down a half-sovereign in Mr. Shaw's for drinks. Witness said he did not believe it and refused to sign it. A further remark was made by Mr. Peacock that it .was the driest election he had I ever seen, and if anybody did throw any money away it I was his nieces. He added it would be a shame to put those orphan girls in the witness box. He told witness that unless he signed the paper his character was gone,l and be was a ruined man, and that witness was the only , man who could save him. Mr. Madden : I don't know how far this comes in the particulars. If you let this statement in you may allow any statement with regard to the respondent. The Commissioner: I don't see how you can possibly shut out the respondent's own statement. I shall keep an open mind on the contents of the statement. Mr. Madden : lam content with that assertion. Continuing, Marshall said Mr. Peacock asked him if Mr. Rushworth had paid for him a gill of beer,to which he replied" No." Whereupon Mr. Peacock said "You are is liar." Mr. Peacock said he had had complaints about witness from men at the gas works, and if he did not sign the paper he would take the matter up against him. Witness said to Mr. Peacock that he could not do anything as he had never done anything wrong, Mr. Peacock threatened to have him ousted out of his job in a month. He asked witness if he was prepared to sign the paper and if he did so be would put £5OO in the bank in his name. Subsequently witness wrote a letter to Mr. Jenkins which was copied from a letter written by Mr. Peacock 49, Dudley.street, Warrington. November 17th, 1908. Dear Sirs,—Re my visit on Saturday last, I have since called on Mr. Peacock and I am pleased to find I must have misunderstood him on Friday last, as I now learn Mr. Peacock was endeavouring to explain that in case of anyone giving false information at the works. Again be says that he would stick up for that which ! was right. I don't want my name to be dragged into I this case if it can be avoided, as everything is now satisfactory.—Yours truly, H. MA FISH ALL. By Mr. Madden: What are you in politics ?—I have been a Liberal. Were you a Liberal or a Tory on the election day ? I was working. - Were you helping Mr. Rushworth ?—Not at all. Will you swear you were not canvassing ?—Yos. When were you in the committee room of Mr. Rushworth ?—Between 5.30 and 0 o'clock. Were you in the Horse and Jockey at all ?—Yes; I 'went with Mr. Rushworth before the election canvassing. You have just told us you were not canvassing for Mr. Rushworth ?—Not on the day of the election. Did you pay any of the workers?—No. Did you and Mr. Rushworth go to different public houses ?—We called at the Wheat Sheaf, Red Lion, and the Soldiers Return. Did Mr. Rushworth stand drinks ?—No I stood them. He gave you the money to pay for them ?—lt was my own money. How much weekly do you get ?-335. Do you mean to say Mr. Rushworth came canvassing with you and was mean enough to let you pay ?—I thought 1 would get it afterwards or I would not have paid for the drinks. You were expecting to be paid by Mr. Rushworth afterwards ?—I have not been paid ytt. How mach will it be for drink ?—I have kept no account. What was the amount of drink paid for by you ?—I don't knew. You got a big offer from Mr. Peacock of £500? You don't seriously ask us to believe such a tale as that ? I have witnesses to prove it. Did it rather astonish you ?—lt did. You didn't believe it, did you ?-1 After the election when did you first meet Mr, Peacock ?—We met by accident. How would the signing of a document stating Mr. Rushworth bad paid 10s. for drinks- in the Red Lion save Mr. Peacock's reputation? What advantage was it to him ?—He said it would squash the case. What did you say to the £5OO offer ?—I said I would not do it that night, and Mr. Peacock said "Consider it over, and call and see me." Did you tell your brother that you had told so many lies you could not sleep ?—No, never. Why did you write the letter ?—I wrote the letter because I did not want to be called in the witness box. Mr. Peacock suggests that you proposed that the letter should he written ?—No. Didn't you dictate the letter yourself ?—No. After the letter was written didn't you read the letter through ?—When Mr. Peacock had drawn it up I read it through. By Mr. Dickens : The only fear was when Mr. Peacock threatened to oust himout of his job. LIBERAL AGENT CALLED. Mr. Joseph Howes, jun., Liberal agent, Said he appeared on subpoena. In reply to Mr. Dickens he said the canvassing books in connection with the election were destroyed the day after the election. Mr. Madden : It is a rule to destroy the canvass books after the election. Mr. Howes said it wan a rule to destroy the canvass books and the Tory agent had told him he destroyed him in the committee room. George James Cooper, iron worker, 138, Longford. street, said on the day of the election he went to vote and on his way he met Alf. Wood at the corner of Silver-street. Wood made the remark, "You know who ' to vote for. You will be all right for a drink after- wards." Witness knew Mr. Wood was working for Mr. Peacock. After voting he went into the Unicorn Inn, where he saw Wood who asked him to have a drink. Witness ordered a glass of whisky but he did not pay for it as he supposed Mr. Wood paid for it. After- wards Wood asked him to.have another which he did and be then left the house. This occurred about ten o'clock in the morning. ALLEGED INTIMIDATIQN. MR. WP. R YLANDS' PRESENCE OBJECTED TO. At this point Mr. W. P. Rylands entered the Court and immediately took a seat directly in front of the -witness Cooper. Mr. W. Madden strongly resented this action. He characterized it as a disgraceful proceeding. It was intimidation and nothing else, and it would be his duty to lay stress upon that fact afterwards. Mr. Dickens; Ridiculous nonsense. Mr. Madden: I object to Mr. Rylands sitting in front of the witness. He is a director of the firm with 'which this witness is employed. Mr. Dickens : Mr. Rylands had not the slightest notion that the witness was going to be called. Mr. Rylands: I had not. The Commissioner: I don't think there is any necessity to make any. charge. The inquiry is being conducted in a most impartial way. Mr. Rylands left the Court temporarily. Continuing, witness Cooper stated in cross-examina- tion by Mr. Madden that he and Wood had often stood drinks together. It was Wood's turn to stand drinks thia time.

whisky before him. Cooper said "I an a Conservative ! but I have voted for Peacock. Al? Wood has paid for this glass of whisky." When Wood paid for witness's drinks-, he produced gold from his pocket. Dumbell and Herbert Davies were canvassing for Peacock on the election day. By Mr. Rees: Witness was wearing the Conserva- tive Association badge on the election day, but no colours. He was in the Horse and Jockey at 7.30 in the morning and had some whisky which he paid for. Ho did not go there by arrangement. He thought there would be something stirring and that free drinks might be had, but there were none. (Laughter.) On leaving the Horse and Jockey he went to the Unicorn and after- wards returned to the Horse and Jockey. Between 7.30 and 8.45 he had five drinks. If Perry says that when he met you at 8.45 you were under the influence of drink, ho would be about right? —No doubt any man would be getting on if he had had five beers. (Laughter.) Further questioned witness said he and Al? Woods were not pals." Witness was formerly a Forester but he did not tell Alf Wood that Peacock had done him a good turn on that Society. "A STRONG CONSERVATIVE." Thomas Knight, 2, Watk in-street, stated that about the Wednesday before the election Air Wood, John Melia (witness's father-in-law) and John Williams came to see him about his vote. Wood said "Wo know you have gut Rushvvorth's bill over your door and that you are a strong Tory, but this is not a general election. It is only the best man for the ward." Witness, however, dicifnot promise his vote, but said he would think it over, and the men left. In about four minutes John Melia his father-in-law, returned and said "Where's your 'bottle " (meaning the beer bottle) and witness told him it was in the corner. Melia took the bottle out and in a few minutes brought it back with a pint of beer in it. He said " Here,get that down you" and went out again. At 12.15. on the election day witness was near the Unicorn Inn when William Dumbell came up to him, wearing a red ribbon in his coat. Ile asked witness if he had given his vote and witness said he would not give it until he had finished his work. Dunabell pressed him to vote then, and witness replied " No. I might get a pint for my vote to-night, when I have finished my work." Dumbell said "Come and have a pint now, and then go and vote and get it done with," but witness did not accept the invitation. Last Sunday night Al!. Wood and Abraham Smart came to his house. Wood was nearly crying and said "Don't press the charge against me. Do your best for me." Witness said he was going to speak nothing but the truth, and Wood' said "Remember I have a wife and five children," and added that if the case went on it would mean twelve months." By Mr. Roes: Witness was a strong Conservative and always would be. (Laughter.) His father-in-law , was a Liberal. When he said he might get a pint for
For Children's tackingeough at night, Wood's Great Peppermint Cure. is. 1. 2s. 91—Advt.
MR. J. A. RUSHWORTH, THE PETITIONER.
Did they say to you at the meeting in the office that so long as you stuck to what you said you would be safe ?—Yes. __

Did you sign a second statement ?—Yes. Was it the second statement you signed in the office in the presence of the manager ?—Yes. Margaret Ann Cooper, wife of the last witness, said Mr. Wood came to see her before the election. WOULD NOT VOTE WITHOUT BEER.

Albert Fisher, brewery labourer, 4, Philip-street, said that on the day of the election either Henry Perry or Arthur Perry first spoke to him about his vote. Sub- sequently he met Wood who asked him if he had given his vote. He told Wood he would vote for neither until he had had a pint of beer. Wood replied that he would see that he got it. When he visited the polling booth he gave his vote for Rushworth. The same even- ing he saw Wood again about 7.30 at the end of Silver- street and he there asked him where the pint was. Wood assured him that he would get it. Later a man named Rose took him into the Unicorn Inn, and he got a drink, and never paid for it. Last week Wood met him, and asked him what he was going to swear. At this stage the Court adjourned for lunch. On resuming, Edward Gleave, wiredrawer, 14, Sharp- street, stated that he left home on the election day at 7.30 a.m. and went into the Unicorn Inn where he had a drink. He then went towards his home. He mot Mr. Perry who said "I have been to your house and your missis has rushed us off.l want you to vote for Peacock. Come on Ted you are all right." Witness said "Oh, ' indeed " and Perry continued : "You can have two pints if you want them, but don't say anything to any- one. You know who to see—Alf. Wood. I will put it all right with All, when you have been in the polling ' booth." Witness went to the booth and voted and afterwards he saw Alfred Wood at the corner of Silver- ; street, along with John Mullen. Perry told Wood " Ted has voted for Peacock—take him in for a drink." Wood said "Have you Ted ?" and he replied in i the affirmative. Wood then said " Go in at the parlour door and I will go round the back" (referring to the Unicorn Inn.) Witness went into the inn and asked for a pint of beer. It was supplied and on witness stating that All Wood would pay for it, he was told it would be all right. "When he had been lathe house for some time. Alf Wood came in and said "Is it right you have voted Ted ?" Witness replied "Yes, I have. I am a Conservative but I have voted for Peacock." Wood then treated him to two more drinks. Before leaving the -Unioa Inn he saw George Cooper, of Longford-street, with a glass of

his vote, he did not expect to get one. George Henry Taylor, 50, Ashton-street, said he saw Knight in company with Dumbell near the Unicorn Inn on the election day. He heard Dumbell ask Knight to vote for Peacock and drinks were mentioned, but he could not tell what Nuts 'actually said. He walked away in disgust. Witness was working for the Socialist candidate.

EXTRAORDINARY INCIDENTS. A WITNESS WHO CHANGED HER MIND. Sarah Ellen Hadcroft, single woman, Smith's-court, a voter in Orford Ward, said that at 12.30 on the election day, Mrs. Silcock, whom she now identified in Court, came to take her to the polling booth. They walked there and after witness had voted they returned in a trap. Mr. Rigby Swift: Before leaving did Mrs. Silcock I give you anything? Witness : No, sir, she never gave me anything. The Commissioner impressed upon the witness to tell ' the whole truth and then nothing could happen to her. Questioned by Mr. Swift, witness said she was in the waiting-room allotted to Mr. Peacock's witnesses during the whole of the previous day and until she was called into Court. Mr. Swift: Before the lady left you at your own ' house did she give you anything ?—No, sir. She never gave me anything. Witness admitted having signed a declaration which stated: "She gave me sixpence when I got-home. She said that it was for losing my time at the cutting shop. I was a quarter of an hour late for my work." The statement, however, was not true. Mr. Swift : Why did you swear it? Witness did not answer. Mr. Swift read as follows from the declaration: "I was a sixpenny piece she gave me. I promised to vote for Peacock previonsly. My family was always Liberal in voting." She admitted swearing to that statement on November 24th. Why did you say this ?—There were two women in the yard talking. One said she had had 10s. and another said she had had ss. and I said "I have t.ad sixpence." Did you hold the sixpence up and say " This is what I got for voting "?—No, sir. What made you say you had got sixpence ?—I only said it in a bit of a lark, the same as they were saying it.

Further cross-examined, witness said she told people in Mr. Peacock's waiting room that it was not true she had received sixpence. he did not tell anybody before Tuesday. Did Mr. Howes, the Libaral agent, tell you you were in the wrong waiting room ?—No. Did he try his best to get you to go out of Mr. Peacock's room? Mr. Madden : Very honourable of him. Witness made no reply. Did Mr. Howescome and tell you yesterday morning that Rushworth's people were making a fuss about you being in his loom, and wanted you to go out can not remember. Pressed by the Commissioner to give a plain answer witness said she thought she heard Mr. Howes say it; but she replied that she would rather stop in. In answer to Mr. Swift, witness said she had a drink of tea in Mr. Wood's house the previous night. She had spoken to Mrs. Silcock on the matter and had told her she had not had sixpence. No one had told her she might get into trouble for taking sixpence. A fortnight ago she fold Mr. Taylor and Mr. Jenkins that the declaration was true, but that was " to get shut of them." By Mr. Madden: Mrs. Irwin who was boasting of having received 55., was a Tory. W itness said she had received 6d., but only for a lark. Mts Irwin was responsible for some of the statements made in the declaration. Mr.l Madden: Is it because of what the Com- missioner told you about telling the truth that you have now told the truth on your oath ? Mr. Dickens: The declaration was made on her oath.

Mr. Madden: You are all trying to intimidate the woman and I wont allow it. It is nothing but intimi- dation from top to bottom. (To witness) : Have you after the warning from the Commissioner told the truth absolutely to-day ?—Yes, sir. Did that lady ever give you sixpence ?—No, sir. She never gave me sixpence. By Mr. Dickens : When she made the declaration stating that she had received sixpence, she had been placed on oath. The Commissioner : When you signed that declara- tion, or just before you signed, was it read over to you by Mr. Taylor or Mr. Jenkins ?—No, sir. It was not read over to me. Was it ever read over to you ?—No, sir. Has anyone ever told you that when you came into the Court to give evidence you were to say you had not been given sixpence by Mrs.Silcock ?—No, sir. Nobody has told me. The Commissioner: lam not saying where she has told the truth but it is perfectly obvious that on one i occasion or other she must have been guilty of a terrible lie and I must disallow her expenses,whatever else I do. Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, solicitor, said the declaration was read to the last witness very carefully before she signed it, and she seemed to understand what was read to her. No pressure was put upon her and she did not object to anything in the contents. By Mr. Madden : Mrs. Irwin did not suggest any- I thing that Mr. Taylor wrote in the declaration. Lily Hadcroft, sister of Sarah Ellen Hadcroft, said she saw her sister return from the polling booth accom- panied by Mrs. Silcocit. She did not hear anything said about sixpence then, but there was some joking about it later on. When witness asked her sister a fortnight afterwards if she had had sixpence, she told her to mind her own business. Another witness was about to be called when Mr. Dickens said that the Chief Constable had made an intimation to him, in consequence of which he would like Sarah Ellen Hadcroft to be recalled. When the woman again appeared in the box, the Com- missioner said : I want you to understand perfectly clearly that whatever answer you give to me now, if it is a true answer I shall give you a certificate which will protect you from any harm happening to you. No harm can happen to you if you answer this one question truly. On the election day did you have a sixpence from anybody? Witness : Yes, sir. (Sensation). The Commissioner: Who gave you that sixpence. Witness did not answer. The Commissioner : You must tell me now. Who gave you that sixpence ? Witness ; Mrs. Silcock. The Court then adjourned until Thursday morning.

THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. A Missing Document. On Thursday morning, before any witnesses were called, Mr. Madden made a statement with regard to the closing scene in Wednesday's proceedings. Mr. Madden said the witness Hadcroft, of course,was not his. Her examination had been concluded, and she was at the last moment simply giving evidence on the invitation of the Court. It was a strange thing, and if there was anythiug said by the girl afterwards it ought to have been communicated to the Clurt instead of to Mr. Dickens. He was not complaining of the conduct of the Chief Constable ; perhaps it was an error of judgment on his part. The statement, such as it was, was communicated to the opposite side. Mr. Dickens, wisely and with great acuteness, did not wish to put the question hirneelt bat left it to the Court. The girl was not now in Court, and the circumstances in which that statement was made ought to be investigated. He wished the Court to consider the question was not closed. The Commissioner: You will have to make out a very strong case for that investigation. You had the striking advantage of being able to cross-examine her. Mr. Madden : I had the disadvantage of finishing her cross-examination and not being allowed to cross- examine on what occurred afterwards. The Commissioner : I will certainly allow you to make another application. Mr. Madden : I think the Chief Constable ought to have an opportunity of clearing himself. CHIEF CONSTABLE IN THE BOX. The Chief Constable (Mr. M. Nicholls) then went into the witness-box, and stated that when the witness Hadcroft left the Court she was in a state of collapse practically, in his opinion, fainting. He took her down to the inspectors' office, and asked her if she was feeling unwell, to which she replied she felt very nervous. He told her she need not be nervous if she bad told the truth, whereupon the woman said "I did have six- pence.' He came straight into court, thinking the only way to communicate that statement to the Court was to inform the counsel who had been examining her. She was quite in a state of collapse, and when the remark was made he readily thought it ought to be communicated to the Court. _lt was not a case of want- ing to help one side or the other. Mr. Madden : I may be a little jealous. The Chief Constable : She was in such a state of collapse that I could not say whether she was respon- sible for the statement made. This closed the incident. FURTHER EVIDENCE. The first witness called was Sarah Houghton, 7 Clegg-street, a widow, who stated that about two or three weeks before the election Mrs. Silcock came to see her and asked her who she was goir.g to vote for. Mrs. Silcock told witness that if she would vote for Peacock she would take her to vote and bring her back, and they would have a drink on the way. In cross-examination witness said she never bad a drink, and would not have bad one if it had been offered to her. Mr. Rees : She first made a statement with regard to the conversation at the Junior Conservative Club. Mrs. Berry, 127, Forster-street, said she remembered the last witness telling her about what happened between her and Mrs. Silcock. On the day of the election she saw Miss Wilkinson, Mrs. Silcock and Frank Hughes working for Mr. Peacock. THE ALLEGATION AGAINST COUNCILLOR PEACOCK. James -Humphries, 16, Warburton-street, an iron- worker, said he commonly went under the name of James Floyd. On the morning of the election he was standing near the Jockey bridge when he saw Ambrose

Wilkinson who said to him " Are you going to try and get Rushworth in ?" and he replied " Yes, if it is possible." A few minutes later Wilkinson again spoke to him and told him he was wanted. They went together to Mr. Peacock's house in West-street. At the time witness had a piece of ribbon in his coat. Mr. Dickens: True blue.

Mr. Madden : No, dirty blue. (Laughter.) Con- tinning witness said Mr. Peacock then took the blue ribbon from out of his coat and put his own colours in and then gave him a shilling. When the shilling was given to him Mr. Peacock made the remark. You know what to do ;" which witness understood meant he was to vote for him. Wilkinson and himself then left the house, and he walked towards the polling booth. On the way he went inside the Soldiers' Return and had some beer for which he paid. Afterwards he went and voted. When he returned from the booth, he saw Wilkinson in the street. Later he went into the Unicorn Inn, where he had some more beer. He did not sea Wilkinson paying for drinks in the Unicorn. Mr. Dickens : In the declaration you made you stated that Wilkinson paid for it. Is that true ? Witnesa : I am not aware of it. Continuing, he said that on Monday, November 9th he went to the office of Mr. Henry Greenall, and saw Mr. Taylor. In the evening he went to the Horse and Jockey. On the following night he remembered being in the Horse and Jockey about seven °Wool( and whilst there he was brought out by his brother Samuel. When he got-oat-1 side he saw Mr. Peter Peacock, Mr. Alf. Wood and witness's two brother. They had a paper which was already written out which they wanted him to sign, in order to squash the case. They threatened that if he did not sign it he would get six months and get disliked amongst his fellow workmen. The paper was to the effect that they wanted him to say that Rushworth gave him £l5 because he said Peacock gave him a shilling. He told them it was not true and to strike it out. The threat about prison so frightened him that h 3 subsequently signed the paper. After that he was taken to a shop in Church-street and he there signed something. Later he went into the BritanLia Vaults but they refused to serve him. On the way home he met P.C. Newey, Mr. Hayes and Mr. Rushwortb, and eventually he was assisted home by a man named Harding. By Mr. Madden : Da you often get drunk ?—I have my share. At any rate on the morning of the election you were quite sober ?—Of course I was. How many brothers have you ?—Seven altogether. Mr. Dickens : That is not his fault. (Laughter.) Mr. Madden: No. Are you divided in politics am a Tory. Are you sure ?-17es. What about your brother Sam. Is he like you a Tory ?—I don't know. I can't rule him.

Where did you get Mr. Rushworth's colours from ? The Horse and Jockey the night before the election. On Sunday night ?—Yes. Did the customers get them ?—Yes. When you wore in llushworth's on Sdaday night did he stand you a drink ?—No. How was that ?-1E paid for my own. Did you stand a drink for anybody ?—No. Have you mentioned this affair to your brother Sam? —No never.

You don't remember if your brother Sam was sober. You were drunk you know, and probably he is right. Do you remember when you first said anything to any- body about the shilling don't remember telling anybody I got a shilling.

Did iour-brother Sant' tell you he had heard this story about the shilling ?—Not that I remember. Do you remember lying down on the tram lines drunk ?—I don't. If I had been there a long time I would have been killed.
Did you tell your brother SAM you would get six months for signing the wrong document ?—Nothing of the kind.
I mean the document of Mr. Rushworth ?—That one was true.
I put it to you that your brother Sam was speaking about Rushworth's document ?—I never said anything to Sam about that document.
Who was it told you that you would get six months? —Alf Wood.

Did you not tell Mr. Peacock that neither he nor anyone else had given you anything ?—I did not say it. When you were taken to the house of Mr. Wilkinson, J.P., di & he not say to you that he could not take the oath as he was chairman of the Ward Committee ?—I was not told that.

Do you know that Mr. Wilkinson recommended you to go to Mr. Locker's another magistrate ?—Yes. When you got to Mr. Locker's were you not told he was out at a Football Club meeting ?—I don't know. Did you go to another house ?—Yes, it was soine- where in Church-street.

Do you know Mr. S. Wright ?-1-es he is the workingman's magistrate. Did you sign adeclaration there ?—Yes. Do you remember whether the paper was read over to you ?—lt was read over to me but I didn't take any notice.

div.head: MISSING DOCUMENT.
div.p: MISSING DOCUMENT.

Mr. Maiden was proceeding to ask further questions with regard to the declaration when Mr. Dickens asked if he might have the declaration paper. Mr. Maiden : I would be willing to produce it but I have not got it. Mr. Dickens : Oh, Oh! • Mr. Madden : There is no need • for Mr. Dickens to jump up me tl. TnerE, no moro gentleman in the profession than the solicitor instruct- ing me and he will say that the document has been mislaid.

Mr. Dickens : That is a very extraordinary thing. The Commissioner: It you wish to speak of its con- tents you must produce the document. It is desirable that it should be produced in court'if possible. Mr. Madden : I have not got that document here but I can call Mr. F. R. Roberts to prove there was a document.

Mr. F. R. Roberts then went into the box. He said that about ten o'clock at night on the day the petition was delivered to Mr. Peacock he was seated at home when Mr. Peacock came down purposely to see him, bringing with him the petition. There were also one or two other papers. He hurriedly glanced through the petition and also through the papers,one of which was a declaration purporting to be that of a man named Humphries or Floyd. He had no clear recollection of what the declaration contained.

Mr. Dickens : I object to any details. Mr. Roberts: lam not going to give any details. Continuing, Mr. Roberts said to the best of his recol- lection he returned the document to Mr. Peacock, as he thought that it being an original document he ought to have the custody of it. Mr. Peacock's ow u impres- sion was--
Mr. Dickens : I can't have Mr. Peacock's own impression. In reply to Mr. Dickens Mr. 113Lerts said he left the document with Mr. Peacock.
This closed the incident with regard to the missing document..
The- crom-exarnination of Humphries was then continued.
Mr. Madden: On what date did you sign the docu- ment at the house of Mr. Wright ?--I believe it was the 10th of November.
Can you tell me the day you signed a document at the office of Mr. Greennll was on the 9th of November.
Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins stated that it was not true that Hamphries was drunk when he made the declaration on November 9.
At this stage Humphries was asked by Mr. Madden to sign his name. _
The Commissioner: You don't suggest he did not sign the affidavits in his presence? Mr. Madden : No.

Mr. Dickens : As it stands at present Mr. Jenkins has said he was sober when he signed Mr. Madden : lam going to take that signature as the best evidence as to whether he was drunk or sober when he signed the declaration. DONE THE "DOLL TRICK."

George Goulden, 61, Hale-street, said he met Humphries under the Jockey bridge when he stated he had received Is. and had done the" Doll Trick" which witness understood to mean be had received Is. from Peacock's party and had voted for Rushworth. Mr. Reece: Did you look upon it as a joke ?—I thought it was meant on his behalf to be so. CONSTABLE'S EVIDENCE.

P.C. Newey said he was on duty ía plain clothes at the Horse and Jockey on November 9th, about ten o'clock in the evening. The witness Humphries came Moly, with another man, and entered the Horse and Jockey Inn. As witness was standing there a man named James Walsh came up to him and said " Newey there is a case for yrpu of a man entering a public-house when he is drunk.' At the same time Mr. Peacock came up and said "Where is he, Wood" and Afred Wood replied" He has just gone across to the Jockey !" Witness began to suspect something and called Mr. Peacock aside, and said to him .‘ What is the game here to-night ?" Mr. Peacock replied that they were trying to bring an action against him but he was not sure whether it was for corrupt practices or bribery. Peacock further said to witness that " If you can go in the Horse and Jockey and do Rtishworth for permitting drunkenness' the other case will fall through.' Witness went into the Horse and Jockey and saw Humphries talking in the vaults to another man. He watched him for three or four minutes. Humphries was sober and if witness had been a publican, he would have thought he was perfectly fit to be served. When Humphries came out of the public-house Mr. Peacock who was standing outside made the remark that they had soon sobered him. He did not see Humphries have anything to drink in the house. He reported the matter on the following day to his inspector. On the following night about 9.30 he saw Humphries near the Blue Coat School. Humphries was being led home by a man named Harding, in a drunken state. At the time Mr. H. Hayes came along and he called witness's attention to the man. He made the remark that Humphries would have a job to see a paper never mind write on it.

. . By Mr. Madden : Did you know that Humphries had been refused drink at the Rodney ?—No. What was the reason you made an entry in your pocket book. You were not going to prosecute ?—I was told by Mr. Hayes I might be required. The Court then adjourned for luncheon.
For Influenza and Bronchial Coughs,Woods' Great Peppermint Cure. is. lid., 2s. 9d.—Advt.
CASES WITHDRAWN.

On resuming after lunch Mr. Dickens withdrew two cases. The first was that in which Mrs. Walsh was stated to have offered a woman the tenancy of a house in Rick Stamford-street in consideration of her voting for Mr. Peacock. Mrs. Walsh was stated to be ill in bed and he had come to the conclusion that he was not in a position to establish sufficient facts to constitute her an agent. He therefore did not propose to go on , with the case. Humphries had not proved the case of 1 treating against Ambrose Wilkinson and that case also would be withdrawn.
MORE ALLEGATIONS OF TREATING.

Richard Bailey, labonrer, 32, Oliver-street, and a voter in the ward, stated that on the election day he met Williath Rylands Alcock in Silver-street about tea time and asked him for Vtd. for a pint. Ile had never borrowed money from Alcock before. Mr. Dickens: What made you ask him on election day?

Witness : Because I was thirsty. (Laughter.) I suppose you have been thirsty before the election day ?—Many a time. (Laughter.) Witness, continuing, said Alcock took him into the Red Lion Inn and treated him and another young man to drinks. After 8 p.m. witness went to the Soldiers' Rrturn. Arthur Peacock was there and-paid for drinks for seven or eight of them. On leaving the public- house witness saw Arthur Peacock in Winwick-road and asked him for the price of a drink. Peacock said he did not think he had any money but he put his hand into his pocket and produced two threepenny-pieces which he gave to witness. Accompanied by his brother- in-law Philip Thompson witness went into the Unicorn ; lon.

By Mr. Rees : Witness worked at Dallam Brewery. He and Alcock were members of the same tontine club, Alcock being the secretary. Do you look upon it now that you owe Alcock 21d. ? —Yes. I have not had time to speak to him.
et-J.7N. P. PEACOCK, THD RESPONDENT.
MR. WM. MADDEN, IltnßrsTErt (Leading Counsel for Respondent).
proceedings took place on a Thursday night about a fortnight before tho election. Mr. Reed: The particulars give the night as October 29th.

Further questioned, witness said not a word was said about the election at the public-house. Thomas Stockton, salt hawker, 3, Old Gardens, cor- roborated the particulars as to the above incident, but disagreed with the last witness in identifying the Mr. Mr. Peacock who was present. When Messrs. Peter and Arthur Peacock stood up together the witness singled out Mr. Peter Peacock as the gentleman who was in the public-house. Thomas Jones, puddler, 6, Warbarton-street, created some amusement. He kissed the book immediately he entered the box, and after the oath had been administered he began witia groat deliberation : "On the setond of April-" . Mr. Dickens: He must have been a policeman. (Laughter). Examined by Mr. Dickens, witness said that on the the election day he saw Abraham Smart, wearing a red ribbon. There was a conveyance close by and Smart said, " Jump up, Tom, you will be all right." Witness said "I am going to give Mr. Rushworth my vote. He has been very good to my son," Smart said, " All right, Tom. You know your own road best " and that was the end of the incident.
Jane Bracegirdle said she overheard the conversation between Smart and Jones but Jones flatly contradicted her version of it.
Mr. Madden objected to Mr. Dickens calling someone to contract one of his own witnesses, but the Commis- sioner directed the witness to proceed.

Witness then said she heard Smart say "Jump in the cart "and Jones refused and Smart then went away. Mr. Dickens read from the declaration sworn by the witness : •‘ Smart said Como on and vote for Mr. Peacock, you will be well paid and have a good feed. You will get your belly filled." Witness : Yes, he said that but Jones says he did not say it.

div.head: SCVEETS AND COINS.
div.p: SCVEETS AND COINS.

Frances Whittaker, 17, Longford-street, said that on the electioN day she saw a motor car bearing placards "Peacock for ever" stopping at doors to pick voters up. She saw swats thrown from the car. The occupants were wearing red ribbons and photos of Mr. Peacock.
Mr. Dickins produced a badge in the form of a bird which was said to have been worn by supporters of Mr. Peacock.
Mr. Madden: Wby it's a cock-robin—(laughter)—a red breast. -
Mr. Dickens: It is a bad peacock. - (Laughter.)

, Witness continuing said that on the night of the election she was present at the jollification at Smarts house. Alf Wood was there and the company included Councillor and Mrs. Cunnington. A messenger arrived with the intimation that Mr. Peacock wished to see Smart and Wood. They went out and half-an-hour later returned. Wood put his hand in his pocket and

produced a sovereign which he banged on the table with the remark "I am not without a b sovereign yet." When Smart came in he also produced a sovereign, and said" What do you think of that for a day's pay." His wife told him to put it in his pocket; it was what he had sweat hard for.
Minnie Whittaker corroborated as to the incident in Smart's house.

By Mr. Rees: Something was said about a bet and when Wood came in he said he had won the money. Williftm James Irvine, 18, Dudley-street, said he was in Silver-street on the election day and saw a man throw a couple of hands-full of sweets. He could not say whether the man was in a vehicle or not. Mr. P. Peacock and Mr. Hampson, the Socialist caudidate,were standing close by at the time. By Mr. Rees : saw children being taken round in a furry bearing the Tory colours. They were not eating buns. _
Are you a Conservative ?—Yes and proud to be one. I'm a Conservative, my wife's a Tory and my three sons are Conservatives.

What's the difference between a Conservative and a Tory ?—I don't know. (Laughter.) Well if you have any more children I hope they will all be Tories too—They will be if I have anything to do with it. (Laughter.) Harriett Smith, 86, Orford-lane, said she saw Prank Hughes going down Orford-lane in a motor car, bearing the words " Vote for Peacock." Hughes kept a sweet shop. Another gentleman in the car was carrying a bag of sweets which were distributed near Sharp-street. By Mr. Rees: She saw Mr. Rushworth's lurry iith fifty children in, going about the ward. The children were singing and shouting "Three cheers for Rush- worth." They were not feedin,,,,. The words on the lorry were : Daddy has voted for Rushworth who is looking after our schools."

Char-les Frederick Traw-, ironworker, 92, Folly-lane, said be was working for Mr. Rushworth on the election day. He cycled behind a motorcar used by the Liberals and he saw sweets thrown to children who wera playing in West-street. In Winwick-road sweets and coins were thrown. He saw a child pick up a halfpenny and he immediately rode to the committee room and com- plained to Mr. Hayes. He also saw sweets thrown near the booth at 9 o'clock in the morning—he should think 31b. or 41b. were thrown away. Witness was wearing a blue ribbon and George Perry asked him to take it out but he refused. The Court then adjourned until Friday.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

The hearing was resumed at 10.15 yesterday morning. William L. Williams, insurance agent,lo, Steel-street, said he took an active part in the election. In a con- versation he had with Mr. Peter Peacock on the morning of the election witness made use of the remark,"We will win to-day." The respondent's reply to that was, "You will not. You will see where you will be. I will win if it costs 250." PETITIONER'S EVIDENCE. Mr. James Armitage Rushworth, licensee of the Horse and Jockey Inn, said there was not the slightest foundation for the suggestion that he paid Humphries any money to tell the story about Peacock. By Mr. Rees : Who is paying the cost of this petition ?—I have arranged with the solicitors. What are your arrangements ?—We got the Con- servative Association to acquiesce in this action. Who is paying this money ?—I will find it if it. is required. Who found the ~C3OO deposit ?-31-7 solicitors arranged it ; lam prepared to pay. Have you paid a penny of the money ?—Not up to no
Have you been asked for it ?—No. Have you paid a penny towards the witness's fees?
_ Have you paid a penny towards the petition ?—Not one iota.
Who was it decided that this petition should be brought? Mr. Dickens :_ You had _better ask Counsel.

Witness : I first brought it before the Com- mittee and asked for their opinion about certain com- plaints made by di flerent people who said that I had been done down. They unanimously decided to go on with the action.

When it came before the Ward Committee what specific charges had you before you?—l had complaints. What coMplaints had you ?—I cannot remember. Can you give one specific complaint before the Ward Committee ?—I cannot tell you now, they have slipped my memory. Was the case of Richard Bailey with the sixpence and two threepenny bits mentioned before the Com- mitted ?—No, not at that time, neither was the case of Humphries. Is it true Mr. Henry Marshall stood drinks in the Red Lion ?—I never stood chinks.
Have you any idea why Mr. Marshall should expect to get from you a good fat sum for the drinks he paid for on your behalf ?—Not the alightest. Did you stand Marshall a drink during the election? —No.
How many drinks did Marshall stand you ?—I don't know.
Why were you so particular not to stand Afarzhall a drink wished to be careful.
What arrangement did you make with Marshall ? None whatever.

- - Has he ever spoken to you about a big fat sum ?—No, ho never mentioned anything to me. Was it by your arrangement that about fifty children were taken out in a lurry ?—No. - Have you asked anybody who paid for the lurry ?—No. Will you now tell me what it is and who it was who persuaded you to take this election petition.—lt was the complaint of the electors ; as we found things out we brought the matter forward.
Did Mr. Hayes make a lot of complaints to you ? He assisted me in getting the case together. Mr. Williams was another.

• Do you know of anyone who gave a bribe or one case of treating.—Not directly. By Mr. Dickens : With regard to the £3OO I think you have the money ?—Oh yes. Walter Connolly Brooks, a member of the Board of GuardianP, Fennel-street, spoke to seeing George Henry Perry and Arthur Peacock going into the Liberal committee rooms.

Tiii--iii;:it-e;;T—He did not draw the attention of the Conservative agent to what he bad seen, but he drew the attention of a lady guardian with whom he was talking, to the incident, and remarked that he thought it was a new way of electioneering to call at a public- house on the way to the booth. By Mr. Swift: He subsequently told Mr. Hayes of the Conservative party, that bethought he (Rushworth) would be beaten because of Perry taking the men into the public-house. Patrick Glynn, Winwick-road, also gave evidence or agency. in reply to Mr. Rees, witness said he saw Joe Rigby, who said " Stick to your colours, you will be all right for 10s. after it is all over." Witness replied, "1 will not do it for ten hundred bobs." Witness saw Ambrose Wilkinson talking to men and fetching them up to vote. Frank Wilkinson, insurance manager, residing in Liscard, Cheshire, said he resided next door to Mr. A. Peacock. He remembered the election in November last. In the course of a conversation he. bad with Mr. A. Peacock, the question of motor cars was mentioned. , Mr. A. Peacock asked witness where he could get a I motor car from. Witness recommended him to a firm in Liscard. He said be wanted one and he would give 50s. or £3 for the hire of one. Witness replied that it was illegal, to which Mr. Peacock replied "If my brother gets in it will take £3OO to get him out, and I do not think the party will go to that." Oa the morn- ing of the election witness saw a motor car drive up to the house and some of Mr. Peacock's family got into the car. He did not know whether Mr. Peacock was in the car or not. By Mr. flees: When did you go the °Mee of the solicitor for the petitioner ?—A fortnight ago. When did you first know that Messrs. Greenall's had to do with the petition ?—I saw it in the papers on the 13th of last month. Do you want us to believe that Mr. A. Peacock thought that 300 would have to be deposited ? don't want to infer anything which is a lie. He told me that. _ _ _

After lunch, further evidence on the question of agency was given. Mr. Dickens produced Mr. Peacock's nomination papers, bearinq the signatures of Abraham Smart, George henry Perry, William Rylands Alcoa, Herbert Davies, Robert Pemberton, John Mullens. LIBERAL AGENT AGAIN CALLED.

Joseph Howes, inn., Liberal agent, produced the minute hook of the Liberal Committee for Orford Ward Mr. Dickens pointed out that the last recorded. meeting was on October 3rd, 1903, and Mr. Howes said there had been no meeting of the committee since the date given in the minute book. Mr. Dickens : There has obviously been a meeting. He quoted the " Examiner " report which stated that a meeting of the Orford Ward Liberal Committee was held in Silver-street schools on Monday evening, December 2nd, at which a resolution was passed con- grattilating Councillor Peacock on his magnificent victory, assuring him of their utmost contldence, believing that his fair name would still remain untarnished. Mr. Howes said there was no record of the meeting in the book because it was not a meeting of the Orford Ward Liberal Committe,e. As the agent of the Liberal Association he never called a meeting of the committee on that date. - - _ _ . -

May I take it that at this meeting Mr. Arthur Peacock was present ?—No sir. Mr. Dickens then read a circular convening a meeting of workers to be held in Mr. Peacock's committee room on October 9th and signed J. Wilkinson, chairman; J. Howes, junr., agent. Mr. Howes said that was not a meeting of the Ward Committee, and there was no record of it. Witness was present but Arthur Peivaock was not. It was merely an informal meeting to inaugurate the campaign. He had no list of workers at the election, and no list of those to whom canvas books were issued. Mr. Arthur Peacock did not have a canvass book, neither did Miss Wilkinson. He could not say whether other alleged agents whose names were mentioned had books. As the books were given out a list of the names was taken, bnt it was destroyed along with the books immediately after the etc ction.
Do you moan to say your mind is a blank about the meeting ?—No, it is not.

Can you tell me anyone who was there ?—Yes. dare say I can. I was there. (Letughter.) Mr. Dickens, however, could not elicit. from the witness whether those whom he named as agents were present at the meeting or not. At a public meeting in support of Mr. Peacock's candidature held on October 31st Frank Hughes was on the platform. By Mr. Rees: The cover of every canvassing book contained extracts from the Corrupt Practices Act with regard to bribery, treating, undue influence and persona- tion, and there was also a warning in the committee MOM.

William Marshall, brother of Henry IMarshall who had previously given evidence said he got a circular inviting him to the meeting Of Mr. Peacock's workers on October 9th and he attended. Herbert Davies was amongst those present. By Mr. Rees : Before Mr. Peacock came forward as candidate, witness was working for Mr. Rushworth. Hø had been a Liberal all his life. By Mr. Dickens : On November 13th he met his brother and they had a conversation, in consequence of which they went to Mr. Peacock who asked his brother to sign a paper. Mr. Peacock said that if his brother would sign the paper it would squash the case and relieve him of all difficulties. The "cheque business about the £5OO was mentioned. His brother would not sign. In answer to Mr. Rees witness said he went to London on the occasion of the brewers' demonstration against the Licensing Bill. He declined to say whether he paid for his ticket or not.
The Commissioner said that matter had nothing to do with the inquiry. MR. MADDEN'S SPEECH FOR THE RESPONDENT. WARRINGTON UNDER THE HEEL OF "THE TRADE."

Mr. Madden said they had now -reached what was popularly known as half-time. The Commissioner: I hope three-quarter time. Mr. Madden : That will depend very largely upon the extend of my friend's cross-examination of naY witnesses. Continuing, he said probably that was the first petition in which the members of the Bar present had been engaged,with the exception of their illustrious friend Mr. Dickens, who in addition to his other laurels had become a distinguished authority upon the election law. It was an indication of the fight which had been carried on and of the power behind the party which was - presenting the petition, that they had gone so far afield' to bring this illustrious authority upon election la'V there to prove a wretched petition, the bribery and corruption in which in money did not extend to more than 12s. 6d., and including the pints of beer and glasses of whisky the whole thing did not reach the paltry sum of one sovereign. All this time was to be, occupied—and certainly there was no objection on the part of the legal gentlemen—(laughter)—in the interests' of public morality and of the party of purity, at an enormous cost running into hundreds and hundreds of pounds, to demonstrate the freedom from corruption of the Tory party in Warrington and the perfidy and corruption of the Liberal party. He would be told that the question of purity was not confined to the amount, whether it be a farthing or £l,OOO or to the question of a pint of beer or a whole cellar full of wine. It %V 9 not the amount of the bribe ; but the corruption, and it was the purification of the electorate and the vindica- tion of the party that was wanted, to show that they at any rate were fighting in this care with clean hands. He was afraid that when his friend placed Mr. Rushwo-r tb on a pedestal and spoke about the acts of impurity or which the Liberals had been guilty, he could hardlY have had in contemplation the revelations made in the witness box by the man Marshall. He never could have thought that in the box Marshall xvould have turned' round and said that night after night before' the election he and Mr. Reshworth, were visiting almost every public-house in the ward, _Rushworth, of course, never spending sixpence, and never speaking about the election bnt taking bis faithful henchman with him and when he went into thef

_ public-houses the half-sovereign was put on the table and people asked to drink. A man with 30s. or 355. e week and a wife and family to keep would never have attempted to do such a thing unless it was true—as he did tell the truth in that one particular—that he expected to receive this money returned to him )11 91 good lump sum. Unfortunately he had not got it yet. Why ? It would not be safe to have it before the elec- tion petition had been tried. It would be safe for Rushworth to pay Marshall when the case was over. Mr. Dickens had pointed out that the Ward had e population of the poor class who were extremely likely to be bribed and to give way to the totuptationof treating. It also had this complexion : that if it had a number of people who were easilY bought by the small sum and the pot of beer, it also made it easy for those who represented a particular interest to go amongst that people; living amongst them, with public-houses planted all over that ward, public-houses belonging to one firm only, the candidate himself a tenant of that firm, bringing UP here as witnesses publicans who also were licensee° under that firm. What might be true with regard te the conditions in other parts of the country had e double emphasis in Warrington which WilS the citadel or fortress of the North with regard to the brewing trade. Amongst those who bad stood up for cleats citizenship against all odds in a town like this, which was so much under the heel of the drink trade,—all the,. more reason why they should be commended ancr supported by all right thinking men in resist- ing ideas which corrupted and under-mined good government—were the two brothers Peacock. They were men who were a credit to their native town- They had sprung from the ranks and perhaps they were ambitious, but he knew no higher thing in a man's life, than civic ambition. It might be a source of persona' gratification but it was coupled with benefit to the community and it was for the good of their fellow men'. Mr. -Madden continuing, referred to Mr. Peter Peacock. It the election he felt that there was e distinct issue between him and not only the Conservative, party but a certain class of interest \vhich was engage° upon the other side. Ile felt he was particularly the man who would be fought most vigorously by the publican party and interest ire the town. Mr. Peacoolc won by a substantial majority. The other side had not the courage to claim the seat.- Instead of the scrutiny being the reasons which deterred them, they knew that if they he' claimed the seat, the Liberals could have met tbeul with recriminatory charges. It was because they knee: of Marshall's conduct about treating people, and 0 other evidence which could have been produced tbst they had not the courage to come forward. Election° had been fought in this town time and time again!. Parliamentary and Municipal, and like men both side' bad taken their beating. They had net retaliated with the cowardly weapon of a petition. If every election that took place had to depend upon that simple puritY, maxim which had found expression in the judgments 0' the judges that even one little bribe of sixpence or ei shilling would invalidate an election, he woul,`", like to know what seat in the country west i" be safe for the person who was now occuPre in,g it. Candidates were responsible inilaw for the action' of their agents, but they might all the same be the victims of circumstances. It would have been a mud' more creditable thing if Mr. Rushworth had taken hi° beating like a man instead of whining about it. For some days they did not know what they were going tn. do. Somebody was going to take the petition up i whether it was conceived n the fertile brain of the übiquitous Hayes or not he did not know. Certainly i,.t did not come from Rushworth, who admitted that nop one of the bribery charges which formed the backbone of the petition was brought before the Orford Ward Committee when the complaints were made. gr' Rushworth did not know that bribery and corruption were going on. He had not seen a single person among the various agents who had been mentioned doing anything wrong on the election day, and not one of his numeroue myrmidons came to make a solitary complaint to hilUe When the petition was launched, the law said that £3o° must be deposited. Mr. Rushworth was asked if be paid the £3OO. No, why should he.? He bad not beer; injured ; be did not know what was wrong. Who psi' it ?—His solicitors. Mr. Rusbworth said he had not paid for one of the great crowd of witnesses who had been brought. Mr. Peacock had himself contemplated? petition, but no one ever beard of a successfo candidate moving in that direction, and it must also be considered that although he had beeo tolerably successful in life, he was not as yet corn" pletely a millionaire. He had not got £3OO to fling about in that manner for the amusement of the Toil party and he had not got a big trade interest at hi°. back. Having enumerated the charges Mr. Madden said no doubt his friends would like something tc. remember the petition by and he had therefore slightlY' parodied an old nursery rhyme : Sing a song of sixpence Two silver bits of threes, A bright and shining shilling, Then fill your pouch with fees ; Some sweets for little children, Rides on a lurry free, Pray tell to rue the difference 'Twixt 'dum and tsveedle-dee. (Laughter.) e Passing on to the evidence, Mr. Madden pointed on' that in one instance they had a statement made id3o° oath, contradited upon oath, and then re-stated. !Sir. Madden had not concluded his address when the Court adjourned until 10.15 this morning.

111 R. RAMSAY MACDONALD AT WARRINGTON. STRONG ATTACK ON MILITARISM AND THE SMART SET. - A demonstration promoted by the Warrington branch .of the Independent Labour Party was held at the Parr Rail on Thursday evening when the principal speakers were Mr. J. Ramsay Macdonald, M.P., secretary of the Labour Party, and the Rev. H. Dunnico, of Liverpool <formerly of Warrington.) There was a fair attendance, Air. James Ball presiding. Amongst those present on the platform were :—Messrs. J. Podmore' E. Highley, W. Carr, J. Houghton, E. Littlewood, R. Wych, C. Parker, C. Hardman, R, Latham and J. Heywood, Miss Johnson, Mrs. Highley, Miss Forster, Mrs. Houghton, Mrs. Rathbone and Mrs. Peadry. Mr. S. Rickers was at the organ. The CHAIRMAN said that if at the last November elections they in Warrington were not successful at the Polls, they could say that they took their defeat in an honourable and proper manner and whatever their faults and short comings might be, and however much people raight differ from them in principles and aims,they could at least say in all boldness and confidence that they fought straight, proclaimed their views honestly and Were willing to abide by the result. (Applause.)

Hnnslet *York - 3 3 15 Leeds *Wigan 4 5 23 Oldham 2 2 10 *Halifax *WakefieldTrinity 0 1 3 Warrington *Swinton 2 5 19 Bradford *Barrow Ebbw Vale 1 2 8 *Bramley Broughton R'gers. 0 2 6 *Nlid Rhondda 0 0 0 Salford 1 4 14 Widnes ... 1 2 8 WELSH LEAGUE. Merthyr Tydvil ... 2 4 16 Barry . . ... 0 0 0 Treherbert Warrington at Wakefield. —A Narrow Defeat. Warrington made their second journey into Yorkshire on Saturday, their opponents being Wakefield Trinity. Both sides were strongly represented, the only changes being P. Boardman and Naylor for O'Neil and Dowell on the Warrington side. Frost has made the ground exceedingly hard, and it WAS a question whether it Was really fit for play, but the referee decided it must pro- ceed. There was only a small gate of about 2,500, but a very keenly contested and interesting match was witnessed. Teams : Wakefield—Metcalfe, back; Bennett, Sldwoll, Lynch, and Simpson, three-quarter backs; Slater and New- bould, half back. ; T. Taylor, Auton. G. Taylor, Cros- land, Parkes, and Walton, forwards. Warrington—Tilley, back; Fish, Dickenson, Taylor, and Treharne, three-quarter backs ; Brooks and Jenkins, half backs ; Chester, Boardman, Belton, Thomas, Naylor, and P. Boardman, forwards. Referee. Mr. W. Mainwaring, Salford. Touch judges, Messrs. H. Adams, Dewsbury, and W. 0. Smart, Hunslee. Thomas set the ball In motion, and the home side was soon on the attack, a strong breeze aiding their movements considerably. Lynch got through in clever style but made a miserable pass when faced by Tilley. Fish responded with a good sprint, but was laid out by a foul tackle by Bennett. Another round of passing between the home backs was well countered by Warrington, and the wing man sent into touch. Play continued in the Warrington half, Brooks and Dicken- son forcing their way to centre was off the field for about ten minutes. Thomas also got in the wars in leading a forward rush. After a fine clearance by Tilley who snapped the ball from the toes of the home forwards. Wakefield settled down near the line. Slater threw out to Lynch who was tackled close in, but grounded over the line. Metcalfe failed at goal. Half-time: Wakefield, one try ; Warrington, nil. On resuming Warrington were quickly on the offensive and some fine punting was ably dealt with by Metcalfe. Fish kicked past the full back and after a run half the length of the field was beaten on the rails by Taylor, the Wakefield forward, who kicked dead. Warrington handled smartly but the inside men seemed afraid to (lash through on the hard ground, and little progress was made. Taylor once looked like sending Treliarne over but the wing man missed the pass when well placed. Simpson got clear away on the home left and a great race was seen between him and Taylor' the Warrington centre overhauling his man ten yards from the line. Warrington rushed back again and the ball coming out of the ruck to Thomas there was a glorious chance cf%coring as the Warring ton backs were all up. Thomas passed badly and the ball was dropped, and with it went Warrington's last chance of winning. Wake- field rushed to the other end and Sidwell• was only just prevented from crossing. Final : Wakefield, one try (3 points) ; Warrington, nil. BARROW v. ST. HELENS. Played at Cavendish Park, Barrow, before 1,500 spec- tators. The turf was in good condition' although a trifle hard, and play was fast throughout. Kelly opened play out to his three-quarters, but Flannigan was tackled by Barnber. Barton had a futile shot at goal, and as a result of mistielding by Treloar' Kelly again sent the ball to H. Greenwood, who transferred to Flannigan, the latter scoring. Greenwood failed at goal. Barrow replied with several good passing bouts, and just beforo half-time Fox secured on the quarter- line,and scored a try, Gifford missing the goal. There was no further scoring and the game ended in a draw. St. Helens 2 points, Barrow 3 points. SALFORD v. WIDNES. Played at Salford. Widnes have only themselves to blame for their defeat at the hands of the Weaste Club by 14 points to 8 for they missed opportunities. Salford in the first portion scored on a couple of occasions through Mesley and Lomas, the latter improv- ing on one, whilst Moran crossed for the visitors. In the second portion the visitors had the better of the exchanges, but they failed to press home their advan- tages. The points recorded were two tries' credited to Mesley for Salford, whilst Jones placed a goal for Widnes. Tay.tor o.rod a try. Result :—Salford I goal, 4 tries (14 points), Widnes 1 goal, 2 tries (8 points).

BAPTIST CHURCH, COLBORNE-STREET. Congregational Tea Meeting. The annual church and. congregational tea was held on Thursday evening. A committee of ladies includ- ing Mrs. B. Few, Mrs. Clatworthy, Mrs. Wynne-Jones, Mrs. U. Buckley and Miss M. Heywood bad charge of the arrangements and a large number of the members of the church and congregation sat down at the well- appointed tables. After an interval for conversation and inspection of plans for new premises an adjourn- ment was made to the church where the minister (Rev. R. E. Letheren) .presided over the meeting. Prayer was offered by Rev. .1. S. Ihrghoo. Mr. Letbereh gave a short address on the critical sitiation the church bad arrived at; critical because upon the result of the decisions they would have to make during the next few months the whole future of the church would depend. He was certain that if they were but whole- hearted and united they would be able to accomplish the task they had set themselves to attempt. The Church Secretary (Mr. 11. BucKnY) reviewed the events of the year, of which the most prominent was the settlement of Mr. and Mrs. Letheren amongst them. He spoke in appreciative terms of the preaching too, and said that 12 lead been received into the church, and as many more were on the point of being received, and the congregation was steadily growing. He also referred to the go .d work done by the newly-formed choir under Mr. C. Dawson. Mr. Wysse-Joses (treasurer) gave a financial state.' ment, 'which showed a-defhit of £l3; but remembering the repeated calls that had been made upon them to provide funds for working parties for the Bazaar and extra expenses in connection with the minister's settle- ment, it was on the whole a satisfactory account. Mr. A. S. ELLIOTT and Mr.B. FEW also spc ke, the latter emphas'sing the necessity of supporting the pastor with 103alty and enthusiasm if the work was to succeed.—Mr. LONGSHA w reportel on the work of the Sunday School and Band of Hope; Mr. T. HALL on Missionary Collections, and Mr. T. DAVIS on the newly-formed " Brotherhood," which he said was proving a means of promoting social inter- course among the young men as well as of quicken- inc, spiritual interest by their Sunday gather:ng. Mrs.. Letheren was asked to speak of the work of the Women's Circle and said that though it was not a church organization yet almost all the women and girls sonnected with the church were members of it. She exhorted the church officers to continue to extend a welcoming band toward it. A piece by the members of the Circle and a solo by Mrs. Patrick added to the enjoyment of a most hearty and successful gathering. HIS Glsi APPEARANCE. John Heater, King-street, was charged at the Borough Police Court on Monday with being drunk and dis- orderly the previous night. P.C. Malpas proved the case.—The Chief Constable stated that it was the prisoners Gist appearance. That appearance was the 7th in eight months. Prisoner was sentenced to one month with hard labour.

You do not suggest that the 2A-1. was lent to pur- chase your vote ?—No, far from it. Continuing witness said he voted between 12 and one o'clock and he did not receive the 2.1. until five o'clock. Nothing was said about the Election by Arthur Peacock when he treated the company in the Soldiers' Return. B j Mr. Dickens: Peacock had never treated him before. Philip Thompson, labourer, 7, Antrobus-street,said he saw Bailey speak to Arthur Peacock in Winwick-road and Peacock put his hand in his pocket. Raney then came up to witness and showed him two threepenny- pieces. They then went and had a drink together. Robert Atkinson, glassmaker, 37, Forster-street, gave similar evidence. Ellen Astill, wife of John Astill, bricklayer, cor- roborated. She also said she asked Thompson, who was her cousin, whom he had voted for and Thompson replied, loud enough for Peavock to hear him, "Cheap ale." Mr. Madden: He didn't say which brewery though. (Laughter.) By Mr. Rees: Her husband was a Conservative. Mary Jane Atkinson, wife of Robert Atkinson corroborated. CONFUSION IN IDENTITY. Thomas Barlow' salt hawker, 2, Gough's:yard, Win- wick-street, said that a few days before the election he was in the Soldiers' Return, along with Thomas Stockton, another salt hawker. Two men namad .Thqoph Glover and Thomas Glynn were also present. "Master" Peacock, Herbert Davies and Robert Pemberton were in the tap room. Mr. Dickens : Which Mr. Peacock was it? Witness: The gentleman there (pointin,,t:. to Coun- cillor Peter Peacock). Messrs. Peter and Arthur Peacock were then asked to stand up together and witness indicated Mr. Arthur Peacock as the one who was present in the public house. Continuing he said several people went to the bar for beer and when it was asked who would pay they said "Over there" (pointing to the tap room). Herbert Davies came out of the tap room to the bar and Glynn said: "Herbert. Am I going to have a drink out of that there ?" Davies said "No von can't. I have just spent the last half-crown." ilynn then said " don't get a drink I shall have you up for bribery." Glynn, however, did not get a drink and neither did witness.
